facts.summary: The engine decides when an SSD read starts in two places. Before arrival, each plan is checked every 0.5 s. just_in_time starts the lookup once now >= predicted arrival + W - r - (early_s + 1 s). The predicted arrival comes from the exact gap or the entry's p50, and early_s = p50 - p10, so jit_p50 lands its reads at the p10. It never conditions on idle time. expected_cost conditions the entry's 64-point lognormal support on idle time and picks the start that minimises stall + lambda x room tokens x pin time. It reads early only when r > W. In both rules W is the wait a turn arriving now would see: (queue length + 0.5) / admissions per second over the last 60 s, falling back to 300 s, then to a wait EWMA. It is a point value, not projected to the arrival time, and EC counts the queue only while the GPU is the bottleneck. r = 0.9 s of fixed lags + read-thread ms per page x (own pages + pages already dispatched), plus a 1 s margin. After arrival the turn looks up at once. It joins any staged read; the arrival gate skips turns whose history is already resident and caps lookups at 3. The read is then held until (position + 0.5)/rate - r - 2 s, except at queue positions 0-1. Here r counts the parked reads ahead of it as well. The read queue dispatches by earliest deadline, 'now' reads first, within a 512-page window and a budget of half the host pool. Timed reads stop while pending writes hold 50K tokens. A landed read stays pinned until admission, within a pin budget of 0.3 x the host pool. No phase schedules backward from deadlines, and the pre-arrival r leaves out parked reads and the write hold. In campaign 34, reads the hold released at once still waited a median 30 s parked. On FA3 the best arms barely read before arrival (ec_full 1 read, jit_exact 99, jit_p50 1,208), and the price never moved. On the trace's heavy-tailed gap entries, the paper's threshold F(x|t) >= q would start reads that the engine's own cost function rejects (CPU check). One rule P(G + W <= now + r) >= q would plug in at _check_pending before arrival and at read_not_before / read_deadline after it, where trigger_time is already shared. It needs a distribution of W projected to the arrival time, r taken from the storage queue (parked + in flight + write hold), and a guard against gaps whose hazard falls with idle time.

findings.topic: Before arrival: just_in_time start rule (jit_p50, jit_exact)
findings.claim: A pending plan is re-checked every 0.5 s. admission_at = t_commit + gap + offset + W. A plan whose admission is more than 120 s out waits. Otherwise the lookup starts once now >= admission_at - load - (early_s + 1.0 s). gap is the exact gap (v1 hint) or the entry's p50 (v2 table). early_s is 0 for exact hints and max(0, p50 - p10) for tables when no landing quantile is set, so jit_p50 times reads to land at the entry's p10. Idle time is never conditioned on: once the predicted time has passed, the read starts even if the turn is late. Staging also needs >= 256 missing tokens, < 256 parked reads and the prefetch cap not reached, and a plan stages at most once.

findings.topic: Queue wait W used before arrival
findings.claim: W = 0 when the queue is empty. Otherwise W = (Q + 0.5)/rate, where rate = admissions in the last 60 s / 60 if there are at least 5, else admissions in the last 300 s / 300 if at least 5. Without either it falls back to the EWMA (alpha 1/8) of measured queue waits of admitted requests that had no storage hit, and with neither nothing is decided. JIT takes Q = the whole waiting queue. EC takes the whole queue only when a queued turn with no read of its own has waited >= 0.5 s (GPU-bound), and 0 otherwise. W is the wait of a turn arriving now, a point value, and is not projected to the predicted arrival. read_deadline always uses the whole queue.

r = 0.5 s (alloc lag) + 0.044 s + p x own pages + p x backlog pages + 0.36 s (drain lag), with own pages = ceil(missing/64). p is a seed of 2.5 ms/page (Qwen3-30B-A3B, campaign 11) until the read thread's EWMA of I/O ms per page exists (alpha 1/8, after 8 reads). From then on both per-page terms use the EWMA, refreshed every tick. For the pre-arrival planner and for refetch, the backlog is the pages of reads already dispatched and not yet acked. Parked reads and the write backlog are left out. The lags are fixed seeds. In campaign 34 the logged EWMA had a median of 3.5-3.6 ms/page (range 2.3-8.9).

findings.topic: After arrival: lookup at arrival, join, arrival gate
findings.claim: The scheduler issues the turn's prefetch when the turn enters the waiting queue. If a staged read under the same handle (rid, attempt 0) is parked or in flight, the arrival joins it and returns. Otherwise the gate decides, for planned turns only. 'covered' (chain - matched < 256 tokens): no lookup. 'retry' (room retry due: >= 2 s after a refusal, at most 8, with the c34 switch on): a lookup that does not count. lookups > MAX_REFETCHES = 2: 'capped'. Otherwise 'read'/'reread', which counts. Each turn thus gets at most 3 counted lookups, staging included. The gate runs after the prefetch-cap check.

A parked read of a queued turn (a planned turn, or any turn when the hold is on) gets deadline None ('now') at positions 0-1 or when there is no rate; otherwise now + (position + 0.5)/rate. The hold sets not_before = last tick + (position + 0.5)/rate - [0.5 + 0.044 + p x read pages + p x ahead_pages + 0.36] - 2.0 s. ahead_pages = pages in flight + pages of every parked read sorted ahead of it in this pass, dispatched or held. There is no hold at positions 0-1, without a rate, or when the read is not queued, which covers staged reads. A read parked since the last tick with an unknown position waits one pass. The hold is re-evaluated every pass.

findings.topic: After arrival: refetch of queued turns (case 2)
findings.claim: Each tick, for every queued planned turn: missing tokens are probed every 0.5 s, and in deadline mode there is no trigger-time test. If >= 256 tokens are missing, no read of the turn is under way, >= 0.5 s has passed since the last refetch, the plan is not capped and the prefetch cap is not reached, the Scheduler re-issues the prefetch through the gate. The deadline and the hold then time it. A second read is logged as a re-eviction and capped at MAX_REFETCHES. Paced miss retries are set to 0 under deadline order with the prefetcher on.

findings.topic: A pre-arrival read when its turn arrives
findings.claim: If it is parked or in flight, the turn joins it, and from the next tick its deadline and hold follow the queue position. A JIT staged read whose p50 deadline had passed, and so had become 'now', is timed again, and a parked staged read can now be held. If it has landed and is pinned, the gate says 'covered' and the pin lasts until admission. EC's release of passed entries and soft-pin bumping stop applying once the turn has arrived. Admission passes over a turn while any read of it, parked or in flight, is under way (wait_complete).

findings.topic: Pins: how long and what can take them
findings.claim: Every landed storage read under the deadline order is pinned at insertion if pinned + its tokens <= 0.3 x the host pool (488,294 tokens in c34); otherwise the pin is skipped (17 times in c34 jit_p50). The pin is released at admission (load-back init, cache_unfinished_req, cache_finished_req), at abort, on replacement, and after 600 s. JIT also releases it at plan expiry (643 expiries in c34 jit_p50). EC releases it once the entry has passed, and soft pins bump it. Bumps take only landed, not-in-flight staged pins of turns not yet queued, for a queued turn's read short of room, least likely to return within one read time first. Eviction cannot take a pinned node, and an arrived turn's pin is never bumped.

findings.claim: Reads and writes run on separate threads with separate queues: a lookup thread (batch_exists), one read I/O thread on the FIFO prefetch_buffer, an ack thread, and one write thread on backup_queue. The cache's HybridCacheController merges queued writes into NIXL writes of up to 128 pages in c34. The two only interact through the write hold and through the read EWMA, which measures read I/O under whatever writes overlap it.

No backward scheduling exists. The pre-arrival planner and refetch see only pages already dispatched. The hold also sees the parked reads ahead in deadline order at that pass. Neither sees reads that will be parked later with earlier deadlines ('now' reads of turns reaching positions 0-1, arrivals' own reads) or the write hold. Nothing checks whether the pages due before a deadline can be read in time.

Time from park to dispatch: timed reads that were never logged as held, so due at once, waited a median 30.2 s (ec_full, p90 48.6 s) and 33.7 s (jit_exact, p90 51.1 s). Held reads waited a median 9.9-10.4 s; reads parked as 'now' waited about 0. In the census for the second half of each run: a median 12 parked reads (p90 31; jit_p50 34), a median 48K tokens in flight (about 750 pages, above the 512-page window), and pins with a median of 0 (jit_p50 154K, p90 325K). The queue in front of the read thread, which the pre-arrival r leaves out, ran to tens of seconds. That the 512-page window was the binding limit, rather than the budget or the write hold, is inferred from the census.

First hold per request (one ntp_hold line each): ec_full 910 holds, at a median queue position of 29 (p90 46), with predicted wait 12.4 s, load estimate 5.6 s and hold 3.8 s (p90 8.9 s). jit_exact: 725 holds, median 5.0 s. jit_p50: 338 holds, median 2.2 s. hicache has no prefetcher and FIFO order. It looks up at arrival and reserves the requested span at lookup. Host pages are allocated when the hit drains, and reads queue on the read thread in arrival order. Landed reads get no pin (pin budget 0) and stay evictable until admission; admission is wait_complete. Paced miss retries run every 8 passes, at most 8.

check_hicache_events (queue drain plus read dispatch) runs before the prefetcher's tick in each pass. Deadlines and holds therefore use the previous pass's queue positions, rate and clock (_last_now).

findings.topic: Where one rule P(G + W <= now + r) >= q would plug in
findings.claim: Before arrival: _check_pending is the single per-plan entry, called by _advance_pending; today it branches to _check_pending_deadline (JIT) or _check_pending_expected_cost (EC). One branch would replace both and return 'stage now' (_stage) or the next check time. The math belongs in next_turn_policy.py beside read_start and remaining_gaps. After arrival: read_not_before is already 'land at predicted admission - r - margin' with G = 0 and a point W, and read_deadline sets the dispatch priority; both would use the same quantile of T. trigger_time is already shared by JIT, the hold and the FIFO path, and is the natural single seam for 'start at Q_T(q) - r'. Storage side: dispatch already computes the pages ahead of each read. A scheduler query for 'pages due before deadline d' (parked + in flight), plus the write-hold state and the read EWMA, would give the planner the r the hold sees. Required state: per plan, t_commit, the 64-point support or a point, the offset EWMA, and missing and room tokens. For W, the queue and which queued turns wait on reads; a distribution of W calibrated on ntp_admit predicted vs measured waits; and other plans' predicted arrivals to project W to the arrival time. For r, parked reads with deadlines and pages, in-flight pages, pending write tokens and the write thread's drain rate. For q, lambda from PriceController.

discrepancies: Paper Fetch, eq. fetch: the engine never evaluates F_i(x_i|t) >= q_i = lambda L/(1 + lambda L). It minimises expected cost over the 64 support points (next_turn_policy.py:165-201), and the two disagree on the trace's unimodal, heavy-tailed entries, not only on multi-modal ones. On the tool entry the threshold says read now, at a cost of 1.81 s against 1.10 s at arrival (sim/cost_curve.py). The paper's justification ('F rises as the session stays idle') fails whenever the hazard falls with idle time.

Paper Fetch, r_i = bL_i/beta: the code's r adds 0.9 s of fixed lags (alloc 0.5 s, drain 0.36 s, fixed 0.044 s), a 1 s margin and the pages of reads already in flight. The per-page cost comes from the read thread's EWMA (median 3.5 ms/page in c34), not from bL/beta (next_turn_estimators.py:119-144; next_turn_prefetch.py:1256-1258).

Paper Fetch, W_hat 'from its position in the queue and the admission rate': before arrival the position is the whole current queue (JIT), or 0 unless the GPU is the bottleneck (EC, next_turn_prefetch.py:698-712). It is not projected to the arrival time, falls back to a 300 s window and then a wait EWMA, and is a point value.

Paper Fetch, memory held = L_i: EC charges rent on room_tokens (key tokens not on the GPU), while the read time uses missing tokens (next_turn_prefetch.py:1153-1155, 1161-1166). A parked read holds no pages, only an anchor lock; pages are taken at dispatch.
Paper 'When to plan' (plan when the gap begins, replan when an input changes): the code re-runs the decision every 0.5 s while a plan is pending (next_turn_prefetch.py:997, 1174).
Paper J_i includes recompute rho U(2L - U): read_start's cost has only the turn's own stall (1 s per s) and rent. There is no recompute term and no cost to the requests queued behind.

The paper's Fetch section covers only pre-arrival starts and says a read 'started at arrival' completes before the head of the queue. The engine does not read at arrival: it looks up at arrival and holds the read until (position + 0.5)/rate - r - 2 s (positions >= 2). It also uses earliest-deadline dispatch, a 512-page window, a budget of half the host pool, a pin budget of 0.3 x the host pool, the write hold, the arrival gate and refetch with a 3-lookup cap. None of this is in the paper, though it is the queue-delay-based schedule the user credits with the gain.

Paper Price section: the arms use 'harm' learning (faded harm / faded staged token-seconds, next_turn_policy.py:290-291), not the multiplicative update on demand minus capacity ('room'). There is no cold-start bisection, no recalibration of forecast tails, and no counting of evicted caches with nu >= lambda. Observed, lambda never moved in c32 and c34 ec_full (5e-5) and fell to its 1e-7 floor in c32 ec_exact.

Design note, 'Fetch: starts at T - r_i, where r_i is the read time under the current storage queue': the pre-arrival r leaves out parked reads and the write hold. In c34, reads due at once waited a median 30 s parked before dispatch.

Design note, 'Hold: a landed read stays pinned until admission': this holds only within the 0.3 pin budget (17 skips in c34 jit_p50). Pins are also released after 600 s, at JIT plan expiry (643 in c34 jit_p50), by EC once the entry has passed, and by soft-pin bumps.

open_questions: Should the unified rule keep a global comparison with 'read at arrival' (an argmin, as read_start does) rather than a pure threshold? With T = G + W and a gap hazard that falls with idle time, P(T <= now + r) >= q fires right after the turn ends and pins memory through the tail.

How should W become a distribution? The ntp_admit lines already log predicted (pred_wait_ql_ms, pred_wait_ewma_ms) against measured waits for every planned turn. Calibrating the error from campaigns 32/34 is a CPU-only step, not done here.

findings.topic: Q1 pages with a pending SSD write
findings.claim: A node with a pending SSD write cannot leave host memory. write_backup_storage takes a host lock on the node at submit and adds pending_backup_tokens; _drain_backup releases the lock at the write's ack without checking completed_tokens. The heap orders by node.last_access_time, oldest first. match_prefix stamps the whole matched path to the root. A queued request's prefix is restamped at arrival (_prefetch_kvcache → init_next_round_input) and whenever the FCFS admission loop reaches it, but not while it is skipped for an ongoing prefetch. findings.topic: Q4 how the storage hit length is computed
findings.claim:
1. anchor = last_host_node, the deepest GPU- or host-valid node; start = len(GPU prefix) + host_hit_length.
2. No lookup if the anchor has no host copy and is not the root, or if the span is under 256 tokens.
3. Keys k_j = H(k_{j-1}, tokens of page j), seeded with the anchor's last page hash, so each key encodes the whole prefix.
4. Each key maps to the files <k_j>_<model>_<tp>_<tpsize>_k and _v; all files are queried, then scanned.
5. kv_hit_pages = index of the first page with a missing file.
6. hit = 64 × kv_hit_pages, MIN-reduced across ranks; under 256 tokens it is revoked as below_threshold.
7. At launch it may be cut to the host room.
8. The read completes only the leading run of readable pages.

findings.topic: Q5 seam: eviction by time-to-next-use class
findings.claim:
The class order lives in get_priority (one object for GPU and host). By class:
- (1) ended sessions: exists.
- (2) GPU-mirror copies: reclaim exists only for write_back. Under write_through it conflicts with GPU eviction deleting nodes that have no host copy, and with SSD lookups being blocked at an anchor that has no host copy.
- (3) idle sessions by expected T: registrations are fixed at commit (W from _wait_after_arrival); refreshing them in tick would make W live.
- (4) staged reads: they are pins (host locks) outside the heap, released only after evict_host fails, never for GPU→host copies. Moving them before QUEUED needs a class-bounded evict_host.
- (5) queued requests far from the head: Queued carries only `since`; positions are known in tick.
- (6) near the head: reads at positions ≤ 1 are already 'now', but the resident prefix is unlocked until admission; a host lock on the head's last_host_node would make it unevictable.

findings.topic: Q5 seam: write ordering by eviction likelihood
findings.claim:
backup_queue is a plain FIFO Queue drained by one thread and grouped FIFO. The only point with node context is write_backup_storage (@rank_consensus), called per node at the GPU→host ack. Options:
- carry a priority snapshot (the node's class or T at submit) on StorageOperation into a priority queue;
- or have the scheduler hold submissions and release them in eviction order (the host lock covers held nodes either way).

Constraints: the tree is scheduler-thread state, and assume_stored assumes every stored page's prefix was written first.

Paper design.tex:148 leaves GPU eviction to the engine. In the engine, the next_use/return_chance strategy orders GPU eviction too (full.py:194-229), and under write_through that choice decides which host copies are unevictable mirror.

Paper Retain (design.tex:310-338) ranks by the ν index, with a (1+λL) factor and a max over horizons. ReturnChanceStrategy instead ranks by P(return within a fixed 30 s | idle), with no size or price term, puts unregistered nodes (shared prefixes, branch points, un-hinted) before every scored session, and puts queued sessions last (next_use_eviction.py:246-271). next_use registers only the tail node, so an ended session's body ranks as UNKNOWN.

Paper Preempt (design.tex:266-280) preempts staged reads when no memory is free. The engine first evicts every unlocked host leaf, including the QUEUED-tier prefixes of other arrived requests, and only then releases staged pins (unified_radix_cache.py:3039-3047). It does so only for a queued asker (next_turn_prefetch.py:1304-1305), with r_j = zero-backlog load time + 1 s (1256-1258, 1320). It never fired in campaigns 32 or 34 (0 ec_bump).

The design note's §3 order puts class 4 (staged reads of sessions not back) before class 5 (queued requests). The engine does the reverse: queued-tier leaves can be evicted, while staged reads are pins outside the eviction heap.

The design note's 'A page cannot leave host memory until it is on the SSD' holds for pending writes. It does not hold for failed writes (lock released at ack regardless), refused GPU→host copies, or pages the cleaner deleted later (the tree still treats the host copy as clean).

The design note's 'cleaner ... once the volume is 90 % full, down to 80 %' is the campaigns' l3_extra.json setting. The engine default is 80/70 (nixl_utils.py:64-67; nixl_cleaner.py:21-22), and start_server.sh's default is 30/20 (line 47).

The engine's price charges a refused token RECOMPUTE_S_PER_TOKEN = 1.1e-4 s (next_turn_policy.py:41-44), measured on Triton in campaign 25. The design note and campaign 32 give 0.042-0.044 ms a token on FA3 (results/campaign32/DECISIONS.md:249-252), so on FA3 the price overstates refusal harm about 2.5 times.

Paper design.tex:108-109 says a read holds L_i tokens until its request is admitted. That is true only within the 30 % pin budget (488,294 tokens). Over it the landed span is not pinned (unified_radix_cache.py:3324-3333): 17 skips in campaign 34 jit_p50 and 9 in campaign 32 jit_p50.
open_questions: Is the post-pass rise in fully missed history really head deletion? A per-request trace would settle it: the first missing key of each lookup against the groups each pass deleted (the cleaner logs only counts). The pre-pass baseline (3-10 % of history) mixes in prompts that diverge from the committed key (compaction, recorded vs generated replies).

Class 2 (dropping host copies of KV still on the GPU) needs a decision between exclusive tiering and write_through. Two parts of the engine assume write-through contiguity: GPU eviction deletes a node without a host copy (unified_tree_core.py:1630-1640), and an anchor without a host copy blocks SSD lookups (scheduler.py:3160-3167; next_turn_prefetch.py:1544-1546).

Cleaner order: touch on read (least recently used order at the cost of two utime calls per page on the read thread), or a cache-fed order (ended sessions first, open sessions spared, tails before heads)? Tail-first needs a chain position that page-key file names do not carry.

Write ordering by eviction likelihood: is it acceptable to break assume_stored's assumption that a stored page's prefix is stored too (already broken by head-first cleaning)? And should the priority be a snapshot at submit, or should the scheduler hold submissions and release them in order?

What share of SSD writes is never read back: ended sessions' last turns, generated outputs that the replay never re-sends, turns served from host? It is not measured, and it bounds what skipping writes saves in disk bandwidth and in host memory held by pending writes.
Which pages do the 26-216 ntp_reevict events per campaign 34 window lose, given that landed spans are pinned? Likely the unpinned resident prefix or the generated-output tail of plan.key; not traced.

Does NIXL's POSIX query_memory or READ path ever touch mtime? Not read on the C++ side; POSIX semantics say no. A lookup also stats every file of the requested span, not just up to the first miss (hicache_nixl.py:233-242, 658-664); its cost on long chains is unmeasured.

facts.summary: The records back the user's statement only in part. Almost all of the measured gain over HiCache comes from the queue-based read schedule: reads timed to predicted admission minus read time, pinned until admission, with queued turns' history kept. At 44 users / 70 GB (Triton, x10), pins alone give 3.8 s (79 % of the gap to exact hints), and the queue-state mechanisms add about 1.0 s more. A no-hint engine with both reaches 96 % of the way to exact hints. At 128 users / 160 GB the no-hint queue-aware arm is at 12.07 s, against 27.74 s for the pins-only arm (one run each). On TraceLab, where the queue wait W (about 170-260 s) is far above the read time r (about 3-6 s) and the read line is short, the hold is worth -77.7 s [-85.1, -70.4]. Where the read thread itself is saturated (campaign 28, reads parked 51-66 s), the read line does the timing and the arms tie. Reads before arrival show a gain in one setting only: 44 users / 70 GB, Triton, exact hints, where most turns outside load episodes have W < r. There exact hints are 0.14-0.21 s ahead of no hints (about 3-4 % of the HiCache gap), against a ceiling of 0.14-0.20 s of read-only stall. With realistic hints no gain is shown. A p50 point estimate costs 0.6-0.9 s (campaign 26 and FA3 campaign 34). On FA3 without the write fixes it started the refused-read loop 8-17 minutes early (8.6 s). At saturation, or with 100 GB of host memory, early reads add nothing. Where eviction by forecast was isolated it moved TTFT by 0.1 s at most; protecting queued turns is what mattered. The four write-path fixes are worth 5.8-9.5 s on FA3. At 44 users, 30 GB more host memory (0.52 s for the no-hint arm) bought more than any hint did. On question 2: after the first cleaner pass (minute 87.9-88.3), the three campaign 34 arms had 116 returning requests that lost at least 1,024 history tokens in 22 minutes, against 16 in the 22 minutes before. Of the 116, 65 had every history lookup find 0 (48 starting at the session's first page), 18 found a contiguous run that stopped partway, 17 found the whole history but then hit a deleted file on the read (31 such failures, all after a pass), and 16 made no history lookup. The recompute comes in bursts after each pass (up to 292K tokens a minute) with 2-5K minutes in between. It totals 1.1-1.3 M tokens per arm (1.5-1.7 % of history). The late rise in TTFT starts at minute 85-86, when the 128-user cap binds, before the first pass. Several numbers in the design note have no record behind them: the Nov 20 trace study, 974 of 2,065, and +0.003 s. Others need qualifying: the 0.16 s, the W < r label, the 0.86 s recompute, the 166K, and "rose until the end".

findings.topic: (a) Pins until admission, 44 users, 70 GB, Triton, x10 (LMCache agentic trace)
findings.claim: Read pins carry most of the gain over original HiCache. The hint-free arm with pins was at 1.51 s against HiCache's 5.33 s on 7,410 turns: -3.82 s, 79 % of the gap to exact hints. The within-run interval is +1.4 to +6.7 s, and the gain is 3.9-5.2 s against HiCache's two runs. With paced retries on, pins alone give 1.71 s (75-79 % of the gain). A landed read is lost 2.3 % of the time when admission follows within 0.5 s, and 99.6 % of the time at 15-60 s.

findings.topic: (a) Pin budget when reads land minutes early (TraceLab, Triton, 128 users, 160 GB, x1)
findings.claim: The old oracle read a queued request at once: its reads landed a median 137 s before admission (p90 327 s). 960 got a pin, and 2,295 found the pin budget (0.3 of the pool) full. An unpinned read was gone a median 1.0 s after landing. Of 1,392 returning requests in minutes 30-110, 696 got nothing.

findings.topic: (b) Queue-timed hold when W is far above r and the read line is short (TraceLab, Triton, 128 users, 160 GB, x1)
findings.claim: This is the largest single effect on record. The old oracle (reads at once) against just-in-time with the hold: -77.7 s [-85.1, -70.4] on 2,556 requests (227.4 to 149.8 s), with 55 % more requests a minute. With the hold, reads land 3.1 s before admission (p90 8.6 s), every read gets a pin, and there is one read per request. The median queue wait was 171-193 s against a 2.6 s read (engine estimate 5.6 s). Caveats: the pair also differs in the arrival gate and the old oracle's 120 s lead. Both arms carried defect 2, which the record says adds to the old oracle's loss.

findings.topic: (b) Hold when the read thread is saturated (FreeInference, Triton, 128 users, 160 GB, x1)
findings.claim: The read thread was 83-96 % busy, and deadline order parked reads 51-66 s, so the read line itself delayed reads to just before admission (the old oracle's landed 2.6 s early). The no-hold old oracle is +3.0 s [+2.6, +3.5] ahead of just-in-time; that cost is the gate's lookup cap (defect 1). The hinted arms span 3 s, and the rules chose 'arrival' for all 2,354 decisions (queue estimate 58 s against a 5.9 s read). The hold adds nothing in this regime.

findings.topic: (b)+(d) Queue-state mechanisms with no hints, 44 users / 70 GB and 128 users / 160 GB, Triton, x10
findings.claim: The no-hint engine `nofc_noend` keeps queued turns' history last, gates and holds reads, and re-reads lost history. On 6,715 turns it reaches 0.71-0.72 s (two runs), 96 % of the way from HiCache (5.47 and 6.62 s) to exact hints (0.51 and 0.54 s). Its gain over the pins-only hint-free arm is 1.02 s, paired on 9,703 turns. At 128 users / 160 GB it is at 12.07 s on 8,001 shared turns, against 11.73-12.23 s for the hinted arms and 27.74 s for the pins-only hint-free arm (one run each, different builds). In campaign 23 at 128 users, LRU took a mean 18.3K tokens of history from 36 % of the hint-free arm's queued turns, against about 2 % in the oracle.

findings.topic: (b) Gate and hold, 44 users / 70 GB, Triton
findings.claim: The gate-and-hold step is -0.17 s (4 % of the gain), within-run interval +0.03 to +0.41 s. The arrival hold itself costs 0.006-0.019 s per turn: reads sit parked 0.08-0.13 s after arrival.

findings.topic: (c) Reads before arrival at 44 users / 70 GB, Triton, x10 (the only setting where a gain shows)
findings.claim: Exact hints with just-in-time reads beat the no-hint engine by 0.17-0.21 s on 6,715 turns and 0.14-0.21 s on 11,067. This is shown in all four pairs against rerun moves of 0.04-0.07 s, and is about 3-4 % of the HiCache-to-exact gap. The ceiling is the stall of turns that waited only for their own read when every read starts at arrival: 0.14-0.20 s per turn. With a short queue a read at arrival costs a reading turn about 1.2 s, but only 5-10 % of turns read (0.06 s per turn). Rules 1+3 on three-quantile hints against no hints: -0.06 to +0.06 s on 6,715 turns and +0.05 to +0.14 s on 11,067. That is not shown, given a rerun move of 0.10-0.12 s. The learned price and soft pins show nothing beyond that (ec_r134 0.80 s, ec_full 0.66 s).

findings.topic: (c) Early reads timed on a p50 point estimate: harm by regime
findings.claim: At 44 users / 70 GB on Triton, JIT p50 (reads landing at the p10) is at 1.35-1.60 s against 0.71 s with no hints, 0.64-0.77 s behind. Its pins hold 28.8-31.5K of 44K tokens of room. Landing at the p90 (fq90) gives 0.94 s. Rule 1 gives 0.67 s and is worth 0.68-0.93 s over JIT p50, with intervals clear of zero. On FA3 with the fixes, JIT p50 is 0.62 s [0.22, 1.02] behind ec_full and 0.67 s [0.28, 1.07] behind JIT exact; its early reads hold 136K host tokens at the median (p90 280K). On FA3 without the fixes, 57 % (jit_p50) and 64 % (old oracle) of reads started before arrival. They pinned 208-267K tokens and started the loop 8-17 minutes early: ec_full to jit_p50 is +8.60 s [+7.25, +10.01], of which 8.31 s comes from requests sent in minutes 65-90, the loop's timing.

findings.topic: (c) Reads before arrival at saturation or with ample host memory
findings.claim: They add nothing. When W is far above r the rules never read early: campaign 28 'arrival' 2,354 of 2,354 (58 s against 5.9 s), campaign 29 765 of 774 (168 s against 5.6 s), campaign 26 at 128 users 3,670 of 3,700 (28.9 s against 4.9 s). Exact against p50 hints: -0.9 s [-1.3, -0.4] and -3.7 s [-4.8, -2.6], both in favour of p50 and read as ties. At 128 users / 160 GB the queue-protecting arms are within 0.41 s (2 %). At 44 users / 100 GB, no hints, JIT p50 and JIT exact tie at 0.41 s (+0.001 [-0.01, +0.01] and +0.004 [-0.01, +0.02]). On FA3 TraceLab (unsaturated) the arms are within 0.03 s. On FA3 with the fixes, ec_full (no early reads) against JIT exact is -0.06 s [-0.19, +0.06].

findings.topic: W against r as recorded, by setting
findings.claim: Campaign 28 (Triton, FreeInference): W about 54-66 s against a read of about 1.5 s (estimate 5.9 s), with reads parked 51-66 s in the read line. Campaign 29 (Triton, TraceLab): W 171-193 s against 2.6 s, read line short (parked 3.4 s). Campaign 26 at 128 users: W 28.9 s against 4.9 s. Campaign 26 at 44 users: the early decisions expected a 0.0 s wait, and those left to arrival 3.9 s against a 3.1 s read. Campaign 32 (FA3), minutes 30-60: W 5.8-7.1 s against 0.8-1.1 s per 20K tokens uncontended; the engine's estimates at ec_full's 'wait' decisions were 3.81 s against 4.48 s. Campaign 34 (FA3, fixed): queue wait p50 10.0 s (p90 24.9 s) over ec_full's run, dispatch to landing 2.1 s, parked 17 s at p50. The read thread is about 100 % busy from minute 70 (jit_p50) and minute 90 (ec_full), with reads parked 39-67 s.

Wherever forecast-based eviction was isolated, it moved TTFT by 0.1 s at most. At 44 users / 70 GB, rule 3 alone against next_use on p50 is +0.004 s [-0.11, +0.12] on 6,715 turns and -0.019 s [-0.13, +0.09] on 9,690. Rules 1+3 against rule 1 is -0.02 s [-0.06, +0.03] and +0.10 s [-0.02, +0.32], and four scores sit level at 0.66-0.80 s. The end signal is worth 0.03-0.04 s, not shown on TTFT, but cuts SSD pages by 14-17 % (shown). On FA3 with exact hints, return_chance against next_use left 5.0 % against 3.2 % of histories missing at admission (minutes 30-65). The TTFT difference is -0.16 s [-0.33, -0.02], or -0.07 s [-0.24, +0.10] without the outside-request stall. What does matter is ranking queued turns last. Campaign 29's -15.6 s [-17.0, -14.3] was next_use's overdue rank (defect 2, now fixed) acting through the lookup cap. In the CPU replay at x10, exact next use beats LRU by 7.9 points of reading turns at 70 GB and by under 1 point from 100 GB. Rule 3 never beats LRU with ended sessions first.

findings.topic: (e) The four write-path fixes (FA3, FreeInference, 128 users, 160 GB, x1; campaign 34 against 32)
findings.claim: Paired on the same users: -9.52 s [-11.05, -8.17] (jit_p50), -5.79 s [-6.68, -4.91] (ec_full), -6.18 s [-7.25, -5.23] (jit_exact). Counted to 5,200 s: -4.79, -0.81 and -1.23 s. Mean TTFT in minutes 60-110 falls from 49.9/34.3/36.2 s to 21.8/20.8/20.7 s. The recomputed share falls from 38.0/21.1/24.0 % to 6.2-6.3 %. Refusals go to 0, and the arms serve 13-24 % more requests. The run cannot say which fix is needed: all four were on, one run each, and fix 4 never acted.

Going from 70 to 100 GB: no hints -0.52 s [-0.82, -0.26], JIT p50 -1.17 s [-1.70, -0.67], JIT exact -0.30 and -0.41 s ([-0.54, -0.10], [-0.73, -0.13]). At 100 GB under 1 % of returning turns read from SSD and the three arms tie at 0.41 s. In the pool replay, reads fall by about half for every 5 GB above 70 GB. HiCache was never run at 100 GB.

findings.topic: Exposed read against queue in the wait split
findings.claim: The exposed read is small everywhere. FA3 campaign 32: 0.01-0.16 s of a 5.0-7.2 s mean TTFT on 9,158 shared returning requests (HiCache 0.49 of 33.18 s). Triton campaign 28: 0.50-0.96 s of 33.8-35.4 s. The differences between arms sit in the queue term.

findings.topic: Q2: storage hits around the first cleaner pass, campaign 34 (counts)
findings.claim: Method: returning requests from client.jsonl, with s2h_query (tokens_req, storage_hit) matched by rid. The history part of a lookup is tokens_req minus the new text, where new text = floor64(prompt) - floor64(ideal_cached). Only lookups made after the request was sent are counted. A request counts as lost at 1,024 or more tokens of ideal_cached minus cached_tokens. Before the pass (22 minutes, three arms together): 16 lost requests (0.70 M tokens computed again), only 3 with a zero hit, and 0-0.35 % of history lookups found 0 or a partial run. After the pass (22 minutes to minute 110): 116 lost requests, 3.60 M tokens (ec_full 36 and 1.15 M, jit_p50 37 and 1.14 M, jit_exact 43 and 1.31 M), 94 of them with 16K or more history. Of the 116: zero hit with the lookup starting at the session's first page, 48 (1.63 M); zero hit after an in-memory prefix, 17 (0.46 M); contiguous run stopping partway, 18 (0.35 M); full hit but still lost, 17 (0.51 M); no history lookup, 16 (0.44 M). 3.3-4.5 % of history lookups found 0 or a partial run. 29 of the 48 head-missing requests were sent within 2 minutes of a pass. Their history is a median 33-38K tokens.

findings.claim: `posix_backend open failed ... No such file or directory` on hicache_l3 files, each with a matching `Prefetch operation ... failed to retrieve page` line: 9 in jit_p50, 10 in ec_full, 12 in jit_exact. findings.topic: Q2: shape and size of the cleaner's recompute
findings.claim: The recompute comes in bursts after each pass, not as a sustained rise. ec_full: 102/81/140K (minutes 87-89), 202/125K (99-100), 194K (109). jit_exact: 292K (87), 182K (89), 104-123K (100-101), 185K (109). jit_p50: 175K (88), 142K (91), 150K (101), 123K (110). Minutes between bursts fall back to 2-5K. The average is 52-59K a minute after the first pass against 6-15K before, which is 1.5-1.7 % of history against 0.2-0.4 %. Each pass deletes 39,650-42,200 groups (232-247 GiB), about 2.5M tokens if a group is one 64-token page (inferred).

findings.topic: Q2: the late TTFT rise is the queue, not the cleaner
findings.claim: In all three arms the 128-user cap binds at minute 84-85, and returning TTFT climbs from minute 85-86 (ec_full 17.5 to 21.6 s), before the passes at 87.9-88.3. Minutes after the pass with no burst still run 23-30 s, with 53-64 requests queued. The head-missing requests had TTFTs no worse than their minutes' mean (ec_full 23.4 s against 27.9 s for minutes 90-110). The extra recompute of about 40-50K tokens a minute is roughly 2 s of FA3 GPU time a minute at 0.042-0.044 ms a token (inferred).

findings.topic: Q2: why the head goes first (code)
findings.claim: The cleaner sorts page groups by mtime, oldest first, between the 90 % and 80 % marks. A group's mtime is the newest st_mtime of its files. Reads do not refresh mtime; only writes do, plus fix 1's touch of a skipped page. batch_exists returns the run of contiguous pages from the first queried page, so one missing first page makes the whole lookup 0. A long-lived session's first pages carry its oldest write time. My reading (not verified in code) is that pages read back from SSD are not written again, so sessions served from SSD keep old mtimes.

findings.topic: Q2: what the logs cannot show
findings.claim: The logs do not list which groups a pass deleted, so blaming a zero hit on the cleaner rests on timing (3 zero hits before the first pass, 65 after, 29 of 48 head-missing within 2 minutes of a pass) and on the code's order. A zero hit only says the first page after the in-memory prefix is missing; 17 of the 65 started after an in-memory prefix. A partial hit gives only the contiguous length, not where the later holes are. For the 16 requests with no history lookup, whether the SSD still held their history is not logged; most lost requests were capped after empty lookups (defect 1). tokens_req includes new text, which I removed using the client's ideal_cached.
findings.evidence: event formats in the three server logs (s2h_query rid tokens_req storage_hit; NIXL L3 cleanup counts only); cleaner_hits3.py docstring

findings.topic: Write path sharing the SSD and host memory
findings.claim: Reads and writes share about 2.05-2.10 GB/s on this disk; in campaign 32's loop it was about half reads, half writes. Once reads take the disk, the single write thread manages 3.8-7.0K tokens a second, while FA3 needs 4.2-5.3K. In campaign 34, pending writes hold 0-7K tokens at the median (p90 65-94K) of a 1.63M pool, and the GPU mirror holds 0.65M. jit_p50's read thread is 100 % busy from minute 70 (ec_full from minute 90), with reads parked 37-67 s.

discrepancies: Design note §1 regimes, 'Recorded pace': 'Human turns hold 76-95 % of resume read time; per-tool forecasts hide 0-0.6 % of it (Nov 20 trace study)'. No record holds this. I searched the .md/.out/.txt/.json files under agent_cache/ (outside frozen/), REALISTIC_HINTS.md, MAINSTREAM_REPLAY.md, the campaign 27-29 checks, earlier session scratch folders and the memory notes. REALISTIC_HINTS.md:137 has a different claim: a per-tool hint keeps 50-54 % of the oracle's eviction gain at x70.

Design note §3: 'about half of its landed reads were evicted before use (974 of 2,065 and 1,209 of 2,139 in two runs)'. These counts are in no record. The recorded ones are 979 of 2,009 and 1,144 of 2,032 turns (campaign25/compare_h_rep.out mechanism rows) and 973 of 2,047 (campaign23/gain44/v1_ladder_lost.out). 2,067 and 2,139 are the two HiCache runs' s2h_io key counts (campaign26/checks/verify/method/census_report.out). 'About half' holds.

Design note §3: 'The index alone moved mean TTFT by +0.003 s (campaign 26)'. The record gives rule 3 alone against JIT p50 as +0.004 s [-0.11, +0.12] on 6,715 turns and -0.019 s on 9,690 (campaign26/DECISIONS.md:967-969). The +0.003 in pairs_ec.out is ec_r1 against rules 1+3, a different pair. Also, the engine's return_chance is the chance of return within 30 s alone; the paper's retention index nu_i (the (1+lambda L) factor and the max over H) was never built (campaign26/DECISIONS.md:60).

Design note §3: return-chance eviction 'was 0.16 s slower' in campaign 32. Without the outside-request stall it is 0.07 s [-0.24, +0.10] (campaign32/DECISIONS.md:59-64). The pair (ec_exact against jit_exact) also differs in read timing (expected_cost against just_in_time), price and soft pins, so the difference is not eviction alone.

Design note §1 regimes: campaign 32 minutes 30-70 labelled 'W < r'. The records give queue waits of 5.8-7.1 s against 0.8-1.1 s to read 20K tokens uncontended, which is W > r (mechanisms_findings.txt:178; campaign32/DECISIONS.md:253-254). The engine's own estimates at ec_full's 'wait' decisions were 3.81 s against 4.48 s, so W and r were about equal (mechanisms_findings.txt:104). The record's mechanism is that the short read line no longer delays early reads (mechanisms_findings.txt:214), not that W < r.
Design note §2 table: 'Queue wait (mean) 23.32 s vs 4.17 s' is only the part 'queued, not its own read'. The whole queue wait is 32.63 s against 5.00 s (campaign32/DECISIONS.md:109-113).

Design note §2: 'With an empty queue on FA3, reading 20K tokens takes 0.8-1.1 s against 0.86 s to recompute them'. The 0.86 s is the recompute cost under load. Idle cold prompts cost 0.031 ms a token, about 0.62 s for 20K, so on an idle FA3 GPU recompute beats the read (mechanisms_findings.txt:174).

Design note §2: 'one recompute cost about 80 times what a per-session model charges' and 'the GPU serves requests in arrival order' are inferred, not measured. schedule_policy is fcfs, but wait_complete admission passes over requests whose read has not landed (campaign26/DECISIONS.md:72-75). The closest measured chain is campaign 28's: 5 points more GPU time spent on recomputed history, 5 % fewer requests, 6.7 % longer waits (campaign28/DECISIONS.md:364-367).

Design note §3 'Recency is a weak proxy ... not supported at recorded pace ... idle age gives nearly the right order': no record measures eviction order at x1. At x10 and 70 GB, exact next use beats LRU by 7.9 points of reading turns (campaign26/DECISIONS.md:1113-1114). What the records do show is that the three-quantile score does no better than LRU with ended sessions first (13.6 against 13.7 %). The same applies to class 3's 'at recorded pace the order is close to idle age'.

Design note §3: 'Campaign 32's first refused reads came while pending writes held up to 166K tokens'. 166K is jit_p50's window peak for minutes 30-60 (campaign34/DECISIONS.md:95-97). At the first refusals of the early-reading arms, pins plus in-flight reads held 207-393K against 33-68K of pending writes. The sustained-loop refusals began with 57-158K pending. 0.25-0.5M of host room is accounted for by no logged lock, and the verifiers found that neither pins nor write locks explain the pre-loop refusals by size (campaign32/checks/mechanisms_findings.txt, early_onset C4 and the verify ALTERNATIVES).

Design note §3: 'With rewrites skipped and writes merged, pending writes stayed under 90K'. Campaign 34 ran all four fixes together and cannot say which one kept pending writes down (campaign34/DECISIONS.md:95-97,166-167).

Design note §3 and campaign34/DECISIONS.md:103-105 ('until the end'; 'what remains late ... from minute 88, history the SSD cleaner deleted'): the 290K peak is right (jit_exact, minute 87: 292K). But the recompute comes in bursts after each pass, with 2-5K minutes between them, and totals only 1.14-1.31 M per arm in 22 minutes (1.5-1.7 % of history). The late TTFT rise starts at minute 85-86, when the 128-user cap binds, before the first pass. The record's 'not traced request by request' is now traced: 65 zero-hit and 18 partial-hit requests, plus 31 read failures on deleted files.

Design note §3 eviction class 5 ('queued requests, farthest from admission first') has never been run. return_chance puts every queued turn in one last tier (campaign29/DECISIONS.md:414-419). Class 4 (soft pins) never acted in campaigns 28, 29, 32 or 34. In campaign 26 it bumped 462 staged reads at a cost in SSD traffic, with no TTFT gain shown (campaign26/DECISIONS.md:854-870).

Paper draft design.tex:184-198 takes queue delays as given and folds them into C. The records show W responds to recompute: campaign 32's queue was 23.32 s against 4.17 s at 36 % against 12 % recompute (campaign32/DECISIONS.md:75,109-113), and campaign 28 shows the chain above. The paper's rules 2 and 4 decided nothing in any saturated run: the price stayed at 5e-5 and there were no bumps (campaigns 28, 29, 32, 34).

Paper draft design.tex:326-329 ('Recency is a weak proxy for this in agentic workloads') has the same problem as the design note's §3 claim: no TTFT gain from forecast-based ranking was shown in any campaign.

Paper draft design.tex:107-109 and 128-131: r_i = bL_i/beta, and 'beyond position b/(2 rho beta) reading is cheaper'. The recorded read time includes the read line's queue (parked 17-67 s in campaign 34, 51-66 s in campaign 28). On idle FA3, recompute (about 0.62 s per 20K tokens) is cheaper than the read (0.8-1.1 s), so the cheaper side depends on load (mechanisms_findings.txt:174,230).
open_questions: Which of the four write-path fixes keeps the first refusals away? This needs runs with fix 2 alone and fix 3 alone (campaign34/DECISIONS.md:171-172).
There is no measured run-to-run spread at the saturated FA3 setting. At 44 users the spread is 0.10-0.25 s, so the 0.6-0.7 s JIT p50 penalty in campaign 34 rests on one run per arm.

No setting has both reads and room: at 44 users, 70 GB has reads but only 44K of room, and 100 GB has room but no reads (campaign26/DECISIONS.md:1201-1205). Whether early reads pay when W < r and host room is ample at once has never been tested.
The -77.7 s hold effect on TraceLab is confounded with the gate, the old oracle's 120 s lead and defect 2. A no-hold arm against a hold arm, both without hints, on the fixed engine would isolate it.
No just-in-time arm without hints has run on FA3 (the campaign 28/32/34 setting), so whether hints are needed at all on FA3 is open.

For the cleaner: logging the deleted group keys, or each lookup's first missing page, would confirm that the deleted pages were sessions' heads and separate them from pages never written. The cleaner's share should grow with run length and a smaller volume (one pass about every 10-12 minutes, about 2.5M tokens each); untested.
Where is the 'Nov 20 trace study' (human turns 76-95 % of resume read time)? It should be saved as a record before the paper cites it.

Would a cleaner that orders by time to next use, or that spares open sessions, remove the 65 zero-hit and 18 partial-hit losses? Refreshing mtime on reads would be a cheaper test of the same idea; neither is evaluated.

facts.summary: Nothing that exists today can serve as the simulator, but several pieces can be reused. The only closed-loop discrete-event model, frozen/oracle_scripts_staging/c20_dist/qps_sim.py, admits requests at a fixed 2.4 turns/s, so its queue wait cannot respond to recompute. room_model.py (event-driven, calibrated room of 90K tokens) and evict_replay.py replay one recorded run's timeline, so the queue wait and eviction are held fixed. mock_engine.py is a wall-clock stand-in for client tests, and toy_floor.py is a synthetic floor with no queue. All of them were calibrated on Triton and the older agentic trace, and all read the old 'turn' client format. adapt_runs.py converts the campaign 32/34 runs to that format but drops the hints. None models the SSD write path, host memory locked by pending writes, refused reads, the SSD cleaner, or page-level shared prefixes. Calibration for campaigns 32/34 (the brief's model is wrong): the runs served Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 with bf16 KV, not Qwen3-32B-FP8, so KV is 98,304 B/token and 6 MiB per 64-token page. The GPU pool is 668,096 tokens and binds at 19-23 running requests, well below max_running 64. The host pool is 1,627,648 tokens, of which the GPU mirror takes about 0.65 M. FA3 prefill costs 0.0365-0.0374 ms/token, plus 27-35 ms per batch, plus about 0.25 µs per token per 1K of prefix; all-in that is 0.047-0.062 ms/token. A decode step takes 3.3-3.5 ms + 0.47-0.68 ms per running request + 0.010-0.016 ms per 1K context tokens. There is one read thread (2.4-3.7 ms/page, 4.6-4.9 in campaign 32's loop) and one write thread (3-12 ms/page, slower as reads rise). Both share one SSD that tops out at 2.10-2.11 GB/s for reads and writes combined. The cleaner deletes about 235 GiB, oldest mtime first, whenever the volume passes 90 %, down to 80 %. Workload: 729 Poisson users arrive (0.1/s, at most 128 in session). The client is closed-loop: each request waits for the previous one to complete plus its recorded wait, capped at 1,200 s. 88 % of requests follow tool waits (p50 1.0 s) and 7.6 % follow user waits (p50 64 s). Prompts average 25.5K tokens with 1.1K new; outputs average 280 tokens; 47 % of requests are SWE-bench. Validation targets per arm: requests per minute, TTFT mean/p50/p90, tier shares, history recomputed, and the queue wait, which is about 97-98 % of TTFT. Campaign 32's loop onset minutes are 67/71/79/80/84 for the hinted arms and 39-42 for hicache's storm; campaign 34 shows no loop at all; campaign 28 (Triton) is a second regime where the arms tie.

findings.claim: A wall-clock aiohttp stand-in for the server, not a discrete-event simulator. It runs a three-tier page-level LRU prefix cache (chained page hashes, write-through), admits a request when its pages fit, prefills one request at a time with T = 0.092 + n/1.19e6 + 3.21e-9(n^2 - c^2) s (the Triton 30B-A3B fit) plus host/storage loads at 400K/21.5K tok/s, and decodes each request at a fixed 12 ms/token with no batch contention. It has no SSD queue, no write path and no hints. Its own docstring says nothing measured on it belongs in a paper. Reusable for testing replay_programs.py and for TieredCache's hashing.

Event-driven (heapq), open-loop replay of one recorded run's SSD reads. It keeps the run's arrivals, queue waits, pages to read and re-reads, and varies only read start and revocation. One FIFO read thread serves reads at the run's median ms/page per 10-minute bin plus 10 ms. Timed reads dispatch below a 512-page window; a revoked read retries after 1 s, up to 3 lookups, then recomputes at a flat 9,000 tok/s. Policies: asrun, arrival, oracle, fixed quantile, expected cost (rule 1) on split/histogram/sample forms, soft pins. One free parameter, the room, calibrated at 90K tokens: counts within about ±25 %. No TTFT, no write path. Inputs: campaign 23 (Triton, 44 users, 70 GB, x10 gaps).
room_model.expected_cost_start agrees with the engine's expected-cost solver on 400 of 400 random cases, so it can be reused as the reference implementation of the paper's fetch rule.

Fits T(L) = a + bL + cL^2 to the Triton single-stream sweep (results/probe_moe/probe.log; Qwen3-30B-A3B, bf16, triton) and re-prices room_model's recompute by position, with 1x/3x/7x weights for the queue effect. No FA3 sweep exists for it to fit.

findings.claim: Per-session dynamic program over idle time on a 0.05 s grid (the priced one-session problem), plus a time-stepped simulation of many sessions sharing one hard room with synthetic lognormal gap keys. findings.topic: existing models: qps_sim.py (the one closed-loop DES)
findings.claim: Closed-loop discrete-event model (heapq) from campaign 20. Users arrive, at most C are in session, and the rest wait in a FIFO list. The GPU admits FIFO at a fixed LIMIT of 2.4 turns/s, and the SSD serves reads FIFO at 3.3 ms per 64-token page. Each session is one unit. Eviction follows engine-like tiers (ended, overdue, far, soon); reads are staged within 120 s of predicted admission under a 30 % pin budget, and plans expire at max(60 s, gap). Its docstring lists what is missing: recompute (so the GPU rate does not depend on U), re-evicted reads, retries and storms, the deadline read order, shared prefixes and partial eviction. It also lacks the write path and refusals. Reusable as an event-loop skeleton with user-cap admission.

Eviction replay on a recorded run's own timeline. One pool of M tokens; histories are evicted from their tails, lowest score first. Policies see only the hint entry (p10/p50/p90), idle time and the end signal; only the exact row sees the true gap. M was calibrated to 982K tokens so that LRU reproduces the hint-free arm's 19.4 % of returning turns reading from SSD. It ranks eviction orders and does not predict TTFT. Runs: campaigns 23 and 25.

Analytic, not dynamic. It calls replay_programs.load_trees and the client's own arrival draw to get the exact users who arrive, then applies Little's law with campaign 28's Triton GPU costs (step 11.2 ms + 0.18 ms per request + 0.0357 ms per K context; 0.158 ms per prefilled token). This is the right way to build a simulator's input, but it holds all 3,787 kept trees in memory (run in the container).

findings.claim: One storage read I/O thread serves reads FIFO from prefetch_buffer (prefetch_io_aux_func), one thread answers storage existence queries (prefetch_thread_func), one write thread handles writes (backup_thread_func), plus a sync thread. Backend: NIXL POSIX on /mnt/ssd/hicache_l3. The store is wiped before every arm.

Uncontended reads run at 18.9-25.7 K tok/s (2.5-3.4 ms/page). Saturated in campaign 34 (minutes 70-120) they run at 17.4-18.0 K tok/s (3.5-3.7 ms/page, thread 100 % busy); in campaign 32's loop at 13.0-13.9 K tok/s (4.6-4.9 ms/page). Over minutes 30-110 the campaign 34 read thread was busy 80.4 % (jit_p50), 57.4 % (ec_full) and 48.4 % (jit_exact). The engine's EWMA (alpha 1/8, first used after 8 samples, logged every 64 reads) read 2.99-4.58 ms/page in campaign 34 jit_p50, with two outliers of 6.4-6.5. Uncontended reads take 9-11 ms for small transfers; the campaign 11 fit is 43.5 ms + 2.477 ms × pages.

The engine predicts a read as 0.5 s allocation lag + 0.044 s + s_per_page × (own pages + backlog pages) + 0.36 s drain lag. The 2.5 ms/page seeds are replaced by the read-thread EWMA; the lags are dense-load seeds (about 0.03 and 0.02 s at sparse load).

Campaign 34 (fixed engine, merged writes): the write thread wrote 37.8-45.2 K pages per 10 minutes (≈4.0-4.8 K tok/s, the write-through demand). It took 3.0-3.8 ms/page with reads idle, 4.4-6.0 with the read thread 20-40 % busy and 8.7-11.6 with reads 74-100 % busy, so reads take most of the shared device. Write thread busy: 16-27 % early, 63-78 % late; pending writes peak at 46-79 K per 10 minutes. Campaign 32 (no fixes): write capacity was 3.8-7.0 K tok/s once reads passed ~1.2 GB/s, against a demand of 4.2-5.3 K tok/s (Triton needed 2-3 K). There, write latency rose to 28-44 s with 245-500 K tokens pending.

findings.claim: To reproduce these targets, a simulator needs what no existing model has: (1) a closed-loop client with user cap and slot waits; (2) a GPU whose batch is bound by the KV pool, with prefill time per batch and per token plus a prefix term, so recompute lengthens everyone's W; (3) page-level radix residency with shared prefixes and write-through mirror accounting; (4) one read thread and one write thread on a shared ~2.1 GB/s device, with host pages locked until their write completes; (5) refusals when host room is short, and the MAX_REFETCHES allowance; (6) the cleaner. open_questions: What tolerance should a simulator be held to? The saturated part of campaigns 32/34 was never repeated, and campaign 34's arms differ by only 0.6-0.7 s. Seeds in a simulator can estimate the spread from arrival draws, but only a GPU repeat measures the engine's.

FA3 prefill above 30K tokens: only one cold request at 53K was measured. Is the loaded regression (0.0374 ms/token + 34.6 ms/batch + 0.25 µs per token per K prefix) good enough, or is an FA3 length sweep (GPU time, after the running campaign) needed before the paper states ρ?

How should the shared SSD be modeled? At saturation, reads got about 80 % of 2.1 GB/s in campaign 34 but about 50 % in campaign 32. Is that the device, transfer sizes (512-page read windows against merged 128-page writes), or the one-read-thread, one-write-thread structure? The write-path policies the user wants to compare depend on it.

What held host memory at campaign 32's first refusals? Logged locks covered only 0.2-0.5 M of the 0.98 M room beyond the mirror (campaign32/DECISIONS.md:182-185); the census exists only from campaign 34. A simulator's room accounting may not reproduce the onset minutes without knowing this (radix ancestors of locked nodes, anchor locks of parked lookups).

How should the workload be extracted? load_model.py's route (replay_programs.load_trees over the 662 MB trace, all 3,787 kept trees in memory) gives the exact 729 users with block-level prefixes but should run once in the container off-peak. The client logs hold only what each arm sent in 2 h, which is arm-dependent.

Should the simulator model block-level prefix sharing (17 % of prompt tokens are held by earlier sessions; first requests find 24 % held) and context rewrites (2 % of returning requests add more than 8K new tokens)? Or are session-level units, as in qps_sim, enough to rank fetch and eviction policies?

Which engine behaviours should be replicated rather than idealized: wait_complete admission passing over requests still reading; the MAX_REFETCHES allowance and defect 1's empty lookups (0-17 capped per window in campaign 34); hicache's 8 attempts at 8 s; the write hold; room retry? Each changed results in campaigns 32/34.

SGLang admits a request only if its prompt plus reserved output fits the pool. The simulator needs an admission rule that reproduces 19-23 running at 0.97 pool use; the reservation ratio is not in the records.

designs.position:
I agree that every decision should key on T = G + W, and that pre-arrival and post-arrival read timing should be one decision rather than two mechanisms. I would change the weighting, though. The records and my checks say the gain is the post-arrival schedule: pins, deadline order by admission position, and the hold. Pre-arrival reads paid in one setting only (campaign 26, 44 users / 70 GB: 0.14-0.21 s, results/campaign26/DECISIONS.md:632), and they never fire once W > r.

The reason is a cost the draft leaves out. Admission passes over a turn whose read is still under way (python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py:4010-4012). So a late read only reorders admissions while other queued requests are ready, and its system cost depends on whether the GPU has other ready work. In campaign 34 it did: whenever requests were queued, the KV pool stayed at about 97 % use in every arm and window, so lateness cost no GPU capacity. When the queue is short, a late read is the turn's full stall.

So I propose one expected-cost rule: earliness priced at the memory price, lateness priced at the probability that the GPU starves. At light load it gives the paper's critical ratio on T = G + W. Under load it gives no early reads and a pull rule that lands each read at, not before, admission. In a toy two-queue model that rule tied the engine-like hold when memory was ample (27.2-27.4 s, while pinned memory fell 41K → 5K tokens) and beat it by 16 s when memory was tight.

Three things are missing:
- r must come from the storage queue. The pre-arrival r was 4-6x short once the read thread saturated.
- W should count only the requests ahead that are ready. Near admission this cuts the p90 error from 9-15 s to 2-5 s.
- The closed-loop law R = N/X − Z should be the paper's account of why W depends on the policy (through throughput X), in place of a work-ahead estimator.

On eviction, I agree to treat Preempt and Retain as one decision. I would rank by slack (time until the history is needed minus time to restore it), with the restore cost set by where the other copy is: on SSD it costs a read; if the host copy is the only one it costs a recompute. Writes are jobs whose deadline is host room. Under GPU saturation they should outrank timed reads whenever pending writes threaten the room the next reads need. Fix 3 approximates this.
designs.fetch_rule:
STATEMENT. Keep one read job for each history that a turn will need.
- Its due time T is when admission would take the turn if its history were resident: T = A + W.
- Before arrival, A = now + G, with G the remaining gap from the hint, conditioned on idle time. After arrival, A = now.
- Release the job at the time s that minimises E[c_E (T − C(s))+ + c_T (C(s) − T)+]. Release means park it for earliest-deadline dispatch; host memory is taken at dispatch. C(s) is the landing time.
- There is recourse: a turn that arrives before s is released at arrival.
- c_E = memory price × room tokens.
- c_T = GPU capacity lost per second of lateness. That is the probability that no other queued request is ready when this one reaches the front, because admission passes over a turn whose read is under way (python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py:4010-4012).
- If the hazard of T increases with idle time, this reduces to "release when P(T <= now + r) >= q, q = c_E/(c_E + c_T)".
- The trace's gap entries have a decreasing hazard (sigma_high 1.79 and 1.86; fetch fact-finder's CPU check). For them a threshold fires right after the turn ends and then pins memory through the tail. So keep the argmin with recourse that read_start already computes (python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/next_turn_policy.py:165-201), and add c_T to it.

HOW G AND W ENTER.
- Before arrival, the spread of T is G's spread plus W's error. Under load W dominates for tool gaps (gap p50 1 s against W of 10-30 s). At light load G dominates.
- W = (ready requests ahead + 0.5) / admission rate, counting only queued turns that admission will not pass over. The tick already counts these for room retry (python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/next_turn_prefetch.py:661-667).
- Offline on campaign 34, minutes 30-110, counting only ready requests changes the p90 absolute error of the remaining wait as follows:

| Time before admission | ec_full | jit_exact | jit_p50 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 s | 8.9 → 1.8 s | 10.4 → 1.8 s | 15.2 → 1.8 s |
| 5 s | 9.9 → 4.4 s | 11.2 → 4.3 s | 16.3 → 4.8 s |

- Turns that had their own SSD read waited a median 6.2, 11.8 and 20.6 s longer than their queue position predicted (ec_full, jit_exact, jit_p50).
- Weighting the queue by tokens (a KV-pool model) does not help. At arrival, ec_full: |err| p50 2.5 against 2.6 s, p90 14.9 against 14.3 s.
- A prefill work-ahead sum is the wrong model here. Admission is bound by the KV pool at 19-23 running requests, and decode takes 61-75 % of GPU time (calibration fact-finder; /home/wanhr/sglang/agent_cache/results/campaign34/checks/decode_scale.out).
- No projection of W to the arrival time is needed for tool gaps. W moves a median 0.9 s over 1 s and 3.2 s over 17 s, less than the estimator's own error at 10-20 s (p90 6.9 s). Human gaps are too uncertain to read early for.
- Scripts: /tmp/claude-1001/-home-wanhr-sglang/cf65791c-c7d4-4411-be47-21b43c92b26f/scratchpad/wf_design/designer-scheduling/w_estimators.py and /tmp/claude-1001/-home-wanhr-sglang/cf65791c-c7d4-4411-be47-21b43c92b26f/scratchpad/wf_design/designer-scheduling/w_estimators2.py.

HOW r AND THE STORAGE QUEUE ENTER.
- C(s) = s + lags + p × (pages in flight + parked pages due before T + expected 'now' reads) + p × own pages + the expected remainder of a write hold.
- p is the read thread's EWMA in ms per page, which already absorbs interference from writes.
- Under earliest-deadline order a read cannot land before the work due ahead of it. In overload, its release time therefore does not matter, provided it is parked before the dispatch frontier reaches T.
- Backward scheduling (latest start times over the deadline-ordered list) matters only when the read thread is underloaded. There read_not_before already sums the pages ahead, pessimistically (python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/next_turn_prefetch.py:1448-1481). It lands reads near admission: campaign 34 ec_full, last landing to admission p50 0.8 s, p90 4.1 s (/home/wanhr/sglang/agent_cache/results/campaign34/checks/read_waits_ec_full.out).
- The real gap is before arrival. The pre-arrival planner's r counts only pages already dispatched (python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/unified_radix_cache.py:2334-2337).

|---|---|---|---|
| 30-60 | 5.2 s | 6.2 s | 6.2 s before |
| 60-90 | 8.3 s | 30.3 s | 15.9 s after |
| 90+ | 8.3 s | 52.5 s | 56.1 s after |

- Script: /tmp/claude-1001/-home-wanhr-sglang/cf65791c-c7d4-4411-be47-21b43c92b26f/scratchpad/wf_design/designer-scheduling/staged_reads.py.

REGIMES.
1. Light GPU load, host memory binding (c_T ≈ 1, c_E > 0). This is the paper's critical ratio on T = G + W with W ≈ 0. Early reads pay only with sharp hints.
2. GPU saturated with ready work queued (c_T ≈ 0).
   - No read before arrival.
   - After arrival, release by ready position (a pull rule): start a turn's read once at most K ready requests are ahead of it.
   - K is small (2-8) or equals the admissions during its own read time, never sized from the storage backlog.
   - Reads then land at or just after admission, and pins hold almost nothing.
3. Host memory ample (c_E ≈ 0). Release as soon as the read is known, at background priority.
4. Storage saturated.
   - Earliest deadline by admission order; early release gains nothing.
   - While the GPU is saturated, keep reading rather than recompute.
   - Recompute only when the GPU would otherwise starve and the recompute would finish before the read lands. On FA3, recomputing 20K tokens takes about 0.62 s on an idle GPU against 0.8-1.1 s to read them (results/campaign32/checks/mechanisms_findings.txt:174).

NEW AGAINST THE ENGINE.
- c_T, taken from the ready count. Today read_start charges every second of stall at 1, and the JIT and hold paths use fixed margins.
- Release by ready position after arrival, instead of the time hold with its 2 s margin (NTP_HOLD_MARGIN_S, next_turn_prefetch.py:128).
- W counted over ready requests only.
- Before arrival, r taken from the deadline-ordered queue plus the write hold.
- One function replaces _check_pending (before arrival) and read_not_before / read_deadline (after arrival). The 1 s JIT margin, 2 s hold margin, early_s and 120 s lead horizon become quantiles.
- Early release is gated on c_T > 0. Expected-cost timing's GPU-bound test (next_turn_prefetch.py:698-712) is a binary version of this gate.

EVIDENCE.

From minute 30, whenever requests were queued, the KV pool was at least 90 % used on 98.7-99.6 % of batch log lines and on average 2.6-3.1 % unused, the same in all three arms and every window. Campaign 32 hicache: 3.7-5.0 % unused. Script: /tmp/claude-1001/-home-wanhr-sglang/cf65791c-c7d4-4411-be47-21b43c92b26f/scratchpad/wf_design/designer-scheduling/pool_idle.awk.
- From the records:
  - Early reads paid only at 44 users / 70 GB (campaign 26).
  - They cost 0.6-0.9 s on p50 hints (campaign 26; results/campaign34/DECISIONS.md:145-146).
  - They did not fire in saturation: campaign 28 chose arrival in 2,354 of 2,354 decisions, and campaign 34 ec_full staged 1 read.
  - The large gains came from avoiding earliness after arrival: the hold in campaign 29, −77.7 s (results/campaign29/DECISIONS.md:388); pins in campaign 23, 79 % of the gain.

designs.eviction_and_writes:
PREEMPT AND RETAIN ARE ONE DECISION.
- A staged read, an idle history, and a queued turn's history beyond the ready buffer are all histories held in host memory ahead of their T. Giving one up turns it into a later read, or a recompute.
- Rank them together by slack: a low quantile of T minus the time to restore. Evict the largest slack first.
- The restore cost depends on where the other copy is:
  - Clean on SSD: a read, which costs storage time and is free while the read thread is idle.
  - Only copy (failed write, deleted by the cleaner, refused GPU→host copy): a recompute. That costs GPU time, which under the user cap delays every request behind it.
  - Dirty (pending write): not evictable until the write acks.
- Order in practice:
  1. Ended sessions (T = ∞).
  2. Host copies of KV the GPU still holds. They are free to drop under exclusive tiering, and are 0.65M of 1.63M tokens in campaign 34 (results/campaign34/DECISIONS.md:98-102).
  3. Idle clean histories, by slack.
  4. Staged pins.
  5. Queued histories beyond the ready buffer (slack W − r), only while the read thread has spare capacity.
  6. Never the ready buffer or reads in flight.
- Under the pull rule, staged pins mostly disappear under load, so Preempt matters at light load only. It never acted on FA3: 0 ec_bump events in campaigns 32 and 34 (evict fact-finder).
- Today the engine does the reverse. A read short of room evicts other arrived turns' queued-tier leaves first, and releases staged pins only afterwards; the pins sit outside the eviction heap (python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/unified_radix_cache.py:3036-3077).
- Wherever eviction order alone was isolated, it moved TTFT by 0.1 s at most: campaign 26, and campaign 32 at −0.07 s [−0.24, +0.10] (results/campaign32/DECISIONS.md:59-64). Present the ranking as protection of histories whose T is small and certain, not as a source of gain.
- "Clean" must mean acked complete. _drain_backup releases the write's host lock at the ack without checking completed_tokens (unified_radix_cache.py:3511-3515). A failed write therefore leaves a host copy that eviction treats as safe.

WRITES ON THE SHARED DISK.
- Reads and writes share one device of about 2.1 GB/s (iostat in campaigns 32 and 34), on separate threads with no I/O priority.
- Campaign 34 (calibration fact-finder): write-through demand was 4.0-4.8K tokens/s. While reads kept the disk 74-100 % busy, the write thread managed 5.5-7.4K tokens/s (8.7-11.6 ms/page), so write utilisation was about 0.55-0.85, a thin margin.
- In campaign 32, rewrites of recomputed history (74-93 % of writes) pushed it over, and pending writes reached 515-675K tokens (results/campaign32/DECISIONS.md:171-183).
- In scheduling terms, a write is a job whose deadline is host room: a pending write host-locks its pages (unified_radix_cache.py:2055-2060).
- A late read is free while the GPU has ready work. So under GPU saturation, writes should outrank timed reads whenever pending writes exceed the room the next pulled reads need. At light load (c_T ≈ 1), reads go first.
- Disk priority classes, highest first:
  1. Reads for the ready buffer ('now' reads).
  2. Writes, when pending writes threaten that room.
  3. Other timed reads.
  4. Background writes.
- Fix 3 is a fixed-threshold version of this: timed reads stop at 50K pending tokens and resume at 25K (python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/storage_read_scheduler.py:147-150, 170-181). Its threshold should instead come from the host room the read planner needs, which the census already reports.
- Write order: FIFO is close to eviction order under LRU-like eviction. Reorder only if write utilisation nears 1.
- Cut demand first:
  - skip stored pages (fix 1);
  - merge writes (fix 2);
  - skip pages that will never be read: ended sessions' last turn, and, in this block-trace replay, generated outputs. The replay rebuilds prompts from recorded reply blocks, so outputs are never re-sent (inferred from /home/wanhr/sglang/agent_cache/scripts/replay_programs.py:7-9). That is about 20 % of the new KV per request (inferred: 280 output against 1.1K new tokens, campaign 34 workload).

SSD TIER.
- Deleting an SSD page turns a future read into a recompute, the most expensive eviction.
- The cleaner deletes least recently written page groups between 90 % and 80 % (python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/storage/nixl/nixl_cleaner.py:168-212).
- Keys are chained, so a deleted head cuts off the whole chain (python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/storage/nixl/hicache_nixl.py:658-664).
- Use the same order by T: ended sessions first, then the largest T, tails before heads, and refresh mtime on read.
- Campaign 34 (evidence fact-finder): after the first pass, 116 returning requests lost at least 1K tokens of history in 22 minutes, against 16 before. That is 1.1-1.3M tokens per arm (1.5-1.7 % of history), in bursts of up to 292K tokens a minute. Small in a 2 h run; it grows with run length or a smaller volume.
designs.paper_structure:
Organize the design section as an architecture around one deadline (T = G + W) and two queues (GPU admission and SSD I/O), coupled by host memory.

1. Overview, with a figure: time-to-use estimator → read planner → I/O scheduler, and host memory manager ↔ GPU admission.
2. Time to next use.
   - G comes from the hints, conditioned on idle time.
   - W = ready requests ahead / admission rate, with its measured error.
   - Why W depends on the policy: under the user cap, R = N/X − Z. A policy moves mean TTFT only through GPU throughput X: recompute, and an idle KV pool. This replaces taking W as the constant C.
3. Read release, the main mechanism.
   - Earliest deadline by admission order, memory taken at dispatch, pins until admission.
   - Under load: release by ready position (pull).
   - Before arrival: release only when the GPU queue is short.
   - One cost statement: earliness at the memory price against lateness at the probability the GPU starves. The four regimes are its cases.
   - Read versus recompute is the same rule.
4. Host memory: one ranking of staged, idle and queued histories by slack. Ended sessions first, clean before dirty, never the ready buffer.
5. I/O scheduler: reads and writes on one device; a write share tied to host room; skip and merge writes, crediting upstream precedent (Mooncake skips rewrites).
6. SSD tier: deletion turns a read into a recompute; the same order by T, tails first.

Hint levels (none, end signal, distribution, exact) become what each component falls back on, not separate arms.

Move to the appendix:
- the earliness/tardiness derivation: the critical ratio for an increasing hazard, and the argmin with recourse otherwise;
- the closed-loop derivation;
- the Lagrangian and its weak-duality floor;
- the retention index and price learning, if kept at all. The engine uses harm learning, and λ never moved on FA3: it stayed at 5e-5 in campaigns 32 and 34 for ec_full and sat at the 1e-7 floor for campaign 32 ec_exact.

Drop or restate these claims:
- "F(x|t) rises as the session stays idle": false for this trace's entries (decreasing hazard).
- "A read started at arrival completes before the head, so nothing is read early": the engine holds reads after arrival, and that schedule is the gain.
- r_i = bL_i/β: r is mostly the storage queue (4-6x the planned value in saturated windows), and β is shared with writes.
- "Recency is a weak proxy", and any TTFT gain from the retention index: at most 0.1 s wherever isolated.
- The multiplicative price update as described: not what the engine runs.
- "Storage holds every prefix cache": the cleaner deletes pages.
- "Beyond position b/(2ρβ) reading is cheaper" as a constant: those are Triton constants; on FA3 the crossover is about 33-37K tokens (inferred), and the choice depends on load.
- The motivation bullet on evicting arrived requests: keep it only as "queued histories beyond the ready buffer".
