risks: The toy model is stylized: no GPU tier, no shared prefixes, all-or-nothing histories, a refusal recomputes the whole history, no write path, rough constants. Its regime results are directional until the calibrated simulation reproduces campaigns 34 and 26.

Late reads are free only while other queued requests are ready. A pull rule with too small a K starves the GPU once more turns need reads (more host pressure, a slower SSD). Sizing K from the storage backlog fed back on itself in the toy (89.5 s against 30.0 s for K = 2 with tight memory), so K needs a cap, or must come from the turn's own read time.

Fairness and tails: a pull rule moves delay onto turns that read. In campaign 34 they already waited a median 6-21 s more than their queue position predicted. Means can tie while p90/p99 and per-user TTFT get worse, so report tails and the reading/non-reading split.

A more accurate W on its own makes things worse. Counting only ready requests releases reads earlier (toy: 87.8 s against 46.3 s for the hold with tight memory). The estimator and the target quantile must change together.
The closed-loop law relies on the replay client's user cap. Under open-loop overload W grows without bound, so the paper should cover both regimes and not generalize from the capped phase.

The FA3/FreeInference setting may never exercise the pre-arrival rule. In campaign 34 the queue was empty most of minutes 0-30, when few reads happen, and non-empty from minute 30 on, when early reads stop paying. The paper's evidence for early reads would rest on campaign 26 (Triton) unless a new setting is run.
There is one run per arm on FA3 and no measured spread in the saturated phase. The toy's seed spread (sd about 2 s) suggests sub-second differences between rules need repeats.

Replay artifact (inferred from scripts/replay_programs.py:7-9): block traces rebuild prompts from recorded reply blocks, so generated outputs (about 20 % of new KV per request) are written to host and SSD but never reused. Write-path conclusions may overstate write demand compared with a real agent loop.

Writes-first can starve reads when write demand exceeds write capacity under load. Then only cutting demand helps (skip stored pages, skip never-read pages, merging), and the bottleneck may just move.

Engine coupling the toy does not model: late reads interact with the 3-lookup cap (defect 1), room retry, plan expiry and pin release after 600 s. A pull rule must not raise capped lookups or revocations.

designs.position:
I agree with both ideas, but I would change the unit they are measured in. The records say the gain is GPU time not spent on recompute, so GPU time should be the currency, and fetch, eviction and writes should be stated as comparisons of three marginal costs: GPU time (mu), SSD time (kappa) and host token-seconds (lambda).

At saturation the replay is a closed loop, so mean TTFT ≈ N·g − Z − decode, where g is GPU time per request. In minutes 90-110:
- campaign 32's loop added 0.555-0.565 s of GPU per request;
- the measured recompute accounts for 0.56-0.59 s of it (13.7-13.8 K tokens at 0.042-0.044 ms);
- 73 % of the 71-72 s longer cycle landed in TTFT.
Sources: /tmp/claude-1001/-home-wanhr-sglang/cf65791c-c7d4-4411-be47-21b43c92b26f/scratchpad/wf_design/economics/identity_check.out, built from agent_cache/results/campaign{32,34}/checks/by_minute_ec_full.out and campaign34/checks/fix_minutes_table_c32_ec_full.out.

So once the queue persists, one GPU-second costs about N ≈ 128 TTFT-seconds, not 1 + Q ≈ 77. In a closed-network toy (one first-come-first-served server) the cost was exactly N for a 0.01 s injection at 51-128 users, and 120 against 1 + Q = 77 for a 1 s injection at 128 users (/tmp/claude-1001/-home-wanhr-sglang/cf65791c-c7d4-4411-be47-21b43c92b26f/scratchpad/wf_design/economics/mu_check_d001.out and mu_check.out). An exposed read, by contrast, costs only its own request, because admission passes over it.

(A) T = G + W is the right deadline, but the start time needs a third term, the storage queue V, and an argmin rather than a threshold. In campaign 34's minutes 90-110:
- the 24-28 % of returning requests that read from the SSD waited 45.6-52.2 s, against 18.2-21.7 s for the rest;
- they were admitted 0.6-0.9 s after their last read landed (/tmp/claude-1001/-home-wanhr-sglang/cf65791c-c7d4-4411-be47-21b43c92b26f/scratchpad/wf_design/economics/read_vs_queue_c34.out).
So the read line, not the GPU queue, timed them, and the hold did not bind. Reads before arrival are the light-load corner of that rule, not half of the gain: exact hints added 0.14-0.21 s at 44 users (campaign 26), and reads timed on p50 hints did harm.

(B) Preempt and Retain become one ranking of every host holder by value per token-second. Losing a clean page costs a re-read (kappa); losing the only copy costs a recompute (mu). Writing becomes its own action: write, defer or skip, with a priority against reads on the shared 2.1 GB/s disk. The SSD cleaner is eviction on the SSD tier.

On the theory:
- The per-session separation survives with mu and kappa as Pigouvian prices. It holds as a decision rule, but not as a lower bound in the closed loop.
- lambda should be computed as the value of the marginal host holder, not learned.
- Speculative holds should be capped by measured slack rather than priced, because host memory's cost has a cliff (Weitzman's prices against quantities argument).

What both ideas miss is capacity. The write-through GPU mirror holds 0.65 M of 1.63 M host tokens, and the disk ran at its limit late in campaign 34. Neither is a timing question.
designs.fetch_rule:
STATEMENT
For a history that is not resident:
- Land it at the q-quantile of its admission time D = A + W, with q = lambda·L/(1 + lambda·L). Start the read r̂ seconds before that.
- Before arrival, choose the start time by minimising priced cost over the support of the gap conditioned on idle time. This is an argmin, as read_start already does (python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/next_turn_policy.py:165-201), not the paper's threshold F(x|t) ≥ q.
- Before arrival, spend only measured host slack.

Priced cost of dispatching at time s:
- E[(s + r(s) − D)^+], the own stall, at weight 1. Under wait_complete, admission passes over a reading request. In campaign 34, jit_p50's non-readers waited less than ec_full's in minutes 70-110: 10.3-16.0 s against 14.3-21.7 s (/tmp/claude-1001/-home-wanhr-sglang/cf65791c-c7d4-4411-be47-21b43c92b26f/scratchpad/wf_design/economics/read_vs_queue_c34.out).
- lambda·L·E[(D − s − r(s))^+], the host rent.
- kappa(s)·t·L, the disk time. It is zero when the disk would otherwise sit idle.
- kappa·t·L·P(read never used).
A refusal costs mu·c_rec·L, so a read that could cause one is ruled out by the slack budget rather than priced.

HOW G AND W ENTER
- G is the hint's gap distribution conditioned on idle time: 64 support points, or a single point for exact hints.
- W must be projected to the arrival time, not read now. It is the work ahead, minus GPU service until A, plus other sessions' expected arrivals taken from their G.
- W's spread should be calibrated on the ntp_admit lines. Today's queue-length estimate errs by +0.3 to +0.9 s for waits of 0.5-30 s, but is 19.8 s short for waits of 30-60 s (campaign 34 jit_exact server.log, calibration fact-finder). It lags a growing queue.
- After arrival G = 0, and the same rule times the hold.

HOW r AND THE STORAGE QUEUE ENTER
- r(s) = V(s) + own transfer + lags.
- V = (pages due before D that are parked or in flight, plus the expected write-hold time) / read rate.
- The planner before arrival and the hold after it use the same r.
- kappa is the number of requests whose admission is bound by the read line. Late in campaign 34, 12-31 reads were parked.
- Once V > W, dispatch order is the decision: earliest deadline first while the deadlines are feasible, value per disk-second once they are not.

READ OR RECOMPUTE
Read iff kappa·t_r + stall/U + lambda·hold < mu·c_rec, per token.
- On an idle FA3 GPU (mu = 1), recompute wins for short histories: 0.62 s against 0.8-1.1 s per 20 K tokens (agent_cache/results/campaign32/checks/mechanisms_findings.txt:174).
- With one request queued, reading wins.
- In campaign 34's late minutes (inferred): a 25 K-token read costs its owner about 28 s, plus about 1.4 s × kappa to others, against 1.07 s × mu for recompute. That is close to a tie at mu = 1 + Q ≈ 60, and about a 2× win for reading at mu ≈ 0.73 N. Splitting a history between the read and recompute is worth simulating.

WHAT IT REDUCES TO
- Light load (mu ≈ 1, kappa ≈ 0, W < r; campaign 26): reads before arrival by argmin. With exact hints, it lands at D minus a margin, which is today's JIT exact. On falling-hazard entries (FreeInference tool and user, sigma_high 1.79-1.86), it reads at arrival.
- GPU saturated, disk keeping up (W ≥ r; campaigns 28/29, campaign 34 minutes 30-70): no early reads. ec_full logged 1 'now' among 6,185 decisions in campaign 34. What remains is the hold, with V inside r and a margin set by the price.
- Both saturated (V > W; campaign 34 minutes 90-110): the hold never binds. Dispatch order and bytes read decide the outcome, and early reads only reorder a saturated disk.
- Host at the cliff (campaign 32's loop): the speculative budget is 0, and writes go before timed reads.

NEW AGAINST THE ENGINE
1. r counts parked reads and the write hold. Today:
   - the r before arrival counts only dispatched pages (python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/unified_radix_cache.py:2334-2337);
   - the hold counts the parked reads ahead of it in that pass;
   - neither counts the write hold;
   - in campaign 34, reads that were due at once still waited a median 30 s parked.
2. W is a projected distribution. Today it is a point value at the current time, and the expected-cost path counts the queue only while the GPU is the bottleneck (python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/next_turn_prefetch.py:698-712).
3. q follows lambda·L. Today the margins are fixed: 1 s (next_turn_prefetch.py:125) and 2 s (next_turn_prefetch.py:128), and jit_p50 lands at the entry's p10.
4. lambda is computed, not learned.
5. The speculative budget comes from the census, not from 0.3 of the host pool.
6. When the read line cannot meet its deadlines, it orders by value per disk-second.
The single seam is trigger_time (python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/next_turn_estimators.py:147), with read_not_before and read_deadline (next_turn_prefetch.py:1448 and 1388).

EVIDENCE
- Early reads add at most 0.14-0.21 s, and only at light load with exact hints (agent_cache/results/campaign26/DECISIONS.md:835-876).
- Reads timed on p50 hints cost 0.64-0.77 s in campaign 26 and 0.62-0.67 s in campaign 34 (agent_cache/results/campaign34/DECISIONS.md:145-152). In campaign 32 they started the loop 8-17 minutes early.
- On FA3, ec_full (1 early read) ties jit_exact (99 early reads).
- The threshold form would read the FreeInference tool entry at once: 1.81 s of cost against 1.10 s for reading at arrival (fetch fact-finder's CPU check).
designs.eviction_and_writes:
ONE RANKED LIST (Retain and Preempt)
Rank every host holder by ν = (chance it is needed per second) × (priced loss if it is not resident) / tokens, and evict the lowest first.
- A page with an intact SSD copy loses κ·t_read plus its own stall, (r − W)^+.
- A page that is the only copy loses μ·c_rec. Only copies arise from a write that failed (the lock is still released at the ack, python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/unified_radix_cache.py:3511-3515), from an SSD copy the cleaner deleted, or from a GPU→host copy that was refused.

Order at saturation:
1. Ended sessions (ν = 0).
2. The GPU mirror. Its ν is about 0, but under write_through it cannot be evicted (python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/unified_cache/unified_tree_core.py:2145-2146). It holds 0.65 M of 1.63 M host tokens (agent_cache/results/campaign34/DECISIONS.md:98-102), the largest misallocation.
3. Idle clean prefixes, by hazard × (κ·t_r + stall).
4. Staged pins, by P(return within a re-read) × (κ·t_r + stall). This is the paper's F_j(r_j|t) when κ = 0. When the disk is busy, a preempted read means a full re-read, so preempt the pins least likely to return at all.
5. Queued prefixes far from the head, only when their re-read can finish before admission. This is a hypothesis; keep queued-last while the lookup cap and refusals exist.
6. Arrived pins and only copies: never.

The engine does the reverse at the boundary: it evicts other queued requests' unpinned prefixes before releasing staged pins (unified_radix_cache.py:3039-3047). Expect little TTFT from refining the ranking:
- forecast ranking within idle sessions moved TTFT by 0.1 s at most (agent_cache/results/campaign26/DECISIONS.md:965-989);
- preemption never fired on FA3 (0 ec_bump in campaigns 32 and 34), and in campaign 26 it bumped 462 reads with no gain (campaign26/DECISIONS.md:854-870).
What matters is the boundary between holders whose loss costs μ (recompute) and those whose loss costs κ (a re-read), and pins and queued-last already approximate it.

CLEAN AND DIRTY
A pending write host-locks its page from submit to ack (unified_radix_cache.py:2055-2060), so dirty pages are outside the eviction heap, and the write order decides which pages become evictable.
- Write the next victims (lowest ν) first.
- Defer pages with high ν; they stay resident anyway.
- Mark a page as on the SSD only when the ack covers it.

THE WRITE ACTION
Write page p iff P(it is needed from the SSD after its host copy goes) × (μ·c_rec − κ·t_r − stall) ≥ κ·t_w + λ·tokens·latency + σ, where σ is the price of SSD capacity.
Zero-value writes should never happen:
- Rewrites of stored pages: 74-93 % of writes in campaign 32's loop (campaign34/DECISIONS.md:89-90).
- Ended sessions' last turns: the end signal cut SSD pages by 14-17 % in campaign 26. Today it is read only at commit (python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/next_turn_prefetch.py:513-532).

WRITES AGAINST READS
The disk is one device of about 2.1 GB/s, roughly 21.4 K tokens/s at 98,304 B a token. In its saturated minutes, campaign 34 split it 1.72 GB/s reads against 0.39 GB/s writes; campaign 32's loop split it 1.10 against 1.00 (iostat_vdc.log of both campaigns).
- Dispatch the transfer with the highest value per disk-second.
- A read is worth κ: the requests bound by the read line.
- A write is worth λ × the tokens it frees when host memory is at the boundary.
- Fix 3 (python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/storage_read_scheduler.py:147-150, 170-181) is the threshold version of this rule, and it points the right way.

SSD TIER
The cleaner is eviction on the SSD. σ is the value of its marginal victim.
- Today it deletes the oldest-mtime groups first (python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/storage/nixl/nixl_cleaner.py:183, 270). Only writes refresh mtime, and with chained keys a deleted head cuts off the whole chain.
- After the first cleaner pass, campaign 34 had 65 requests whose lookup found nothing, 18 that found only part of their history, and 31 reads that failed on deleted files. That is 1.1-1.3 M recomputed tokens per arm in 22 minutes (evidence fact-finder).
- By the closed-loop identity that is 17-20 ms of GPU time per request, about 2.2-2.5 s of cycle time and about 1.6-1.9 s of TTFT (inferred; /tmp/claude-1001/-home-wanhr-sglang/cf65791c-c7d4-4411-be47-21b43c92b26f/scratchpad/wf_design/economics/identity_check.out).
- Priced order: ended sessions first, then the tails of the coldest live chains (deleting page j loses pages j through the end), never a live head. Refreshing mtime on reads is the minimal fix.

PRICE λ
Compute it rather than learn it: λ = the smoothed maximum ν among the holders evicted in the last interval.
- With a need rate of about 1/60 s (host turnover is about a minute), late campaign 34 gives about 2e-5, dominated by the disk; early campaign 34 gives about 1e-6; campaign 32's loop gives about 4e-5 (all inferred).
- Today's 'harm' rule cannot move. It charges only refusals up to the staged pins seen (next_turn_prefetch.py:1345-1360). It uses Triton's 1.1e-4 s a token (python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/next_turn_policy.py:44), 2.5× FA3's cost. In campaigns 32 and 34 it stayed at 5e-5 (campaign32/DECISIONS.md:225-226).
- Use λ for ranking and for comparing writes with reads. Govern speculative holds with budgets.

STABILITY
Campaign 32's loop had two causes in price terms.
- A missing price: rewrites were bought at zero.
- Rationing by refusal: a refused read is recomputed, and the recompute is written again, so demand grew with the shortage.
Campaign 34 rationed by delay instead. Readers absorbed the shortage as their own wait (+26-33 s late), nothing fed back into write demand, and no read was refused.

A priced design is stable if:
1. zero-value flows are priced out;
2. a scarce resource is rationed by an action that does not create demand for it: delay a read rather than refuse it;
3. speculative holds come only from measured slack. The fixed pin budget of 0.3 of the host pool did not stop jit_p50's 208-267 K early pins in campaign 32 (agent_cache/results/campaign32/DECISIONS.md:197-200);
4. the mandatory flows fit the device. Late in campaign 34: about 4.3 K tokens/s of writes plus 17.7 K of reads, against 21.4 K.

Damping it needs:
- smooth μ and κ over the dispatch-to-landing horizon, and λ over host turnover;
- hysteresis bands. The 50 K/25 K hold switched on 28-30 times a run, for a median of 2.0-2.8 s;
- a rate limit on speculative starts, since one change in a global price flips every plan at once;
- caps: μ ≤ users in session, and λ ≤ μ·c_rec divided by the shortest useful hold.

Prices cannot create capacity. When mandatory flows exceed it, the cheapest rationing order is delay (weight 1), then skipping low-value writes, then recompute (weight μ).

experiments.method: Simulation arms: today's hold with earliest-deadline-first order; work-conserving dispatch within a slack budget; pre-arrival reads into idle disk time with exact against p50 hints; earliest-deadline-first against value order once parked work exceeds capacity; splitting one history between a read and a recompute when V − W is large.

risks: At saturation, mu ≈ N makes the priced design reduce to 'never recompute', which campaign 34's simple arms already do: they tie within 0.7 s. The novelty has to come from accounting for capacity (host room, the read line, writes). Otherwise the design reads as relabelled heuristics.

Prices taken instantaneously can herd. Every plan sees the same change in mu or lambda at once, so speculative reads would start in bursts. Without slack budgets and hysteresis, a priced design could bring back campaign 32's early onset (inferred).

A calibrated simulation may not reproduce campaign 32's onset. At the first refusals, 0.25-0.5 M tokens of host room were held by no logged lock (agent_cache/results/campaign32/DECISIONS.md:179-184). Any stability conclusion then rests on a fitted cascade factor.

mu is not 1 + Q. Both the toy and the campaign 32/34 identity give about N. An engine that uses queue length underprices GPU time by about 1.6× at the 128-user cap, and by more near the knee, which is exactly where early reads are decided.

The replay's metric, mean TTFT of requests sent before 6,600 s, mixes in throughput. Campaign 34's p50 rose because it served more requests late in the run. A price on summed TTFT can trade away throughput, so report paired TTFT alongside requests per minute.
Each arm ran once, and no run-to-run spread is measured at saturation. Campaign 34's 0.6-0.7 s differences and the loop-onset minutes may be noise.

Constants must be the served model's. Campaigns 28-34 ran Qwen3-30B-A3B with bf16 KV (98,304 B a token), not Qwen3-32B-FP8. The engine's harm price still uses Triton's 1.1e-4 s a token (python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/next_turn_policy.py:44), 2.5× FA3's cost.

Exclusive tiering and reordering writes both break engine assumptions: an anchor without a host copy blocks SSD lookups, and assume_stored relies on prefixes being written first. The largest lever is also the riskiest change.
The 'both saturated' regime may belong to this box: one read thread, NIXL POSIX, a 2.1 GB/s disk, bf16 KV. With more disk bandwidth or FP8 KV it could disappear, and the read-line rules with it.
The toy behind the mu claim is a single first-come-first-served server. Continuous batching splits the cost between TTFT (73 % in campaign 32 against 34) and decode, and its knee is not sharp.

designs.position:
I agree that T = G + W should key every decision, and that the write path and the SSD tier belong in the design. On the fixed engine, though, the storage costs sit somewhere other than where the proposal puts them.

- **Pending writes are not what fills host memory.** In campaign 34 they hold a median 0-7 K tokens. The write-through mirror holds 0.64-0.65 M of the 1.63 M-token pool, and from minute 30 it equals the KV of the requests running on the GPU (0.65 M), so nothing ever reads it from host while it is there.
- **The queue outgrows host memory, and the read line saturates.** From minute 70-80, queued requests' histories (0.9 M, rising to 1.6-1.7 M) exceed the 0.90-0.92 M of host-only room. The excess cycles through the SSD and the single read line saturates. In minutes 90-110, returning requests with a read waited 46-69 s; the others waited 12-19 s.
- **Host accounting should come before forecast-based eviction.** An open-loop replay of the three campaign 34 timelines puts the mirror at 56-61 % of SSD read demand. A perfect next-use order with session ends saves 22-25 %.
- **For (A):** the read start is not a per-read decision. Reads share one device of about 2.1 GB/s with writes, so r must come from the I/O queue (parked reads, reads in flight, the write share). Reads should be scheduled backward from their deadlines. Reads before arrival should run only when the device has slack: jit_p50's early reads raised SSD volume to 82.5 M tokens, against 54-64 M for the other arms, and saturated the read line 20 minutes earlier.
- **For (B):** I would merge Preempt and Retain into one order keyed on slack, T minus (read-line delay + r), over explicit page states: pinned, dirty, clean, clean duplicate. Keep eager write-through, since pages are immutable and each page read back is read 4.2-4.5 times. Stop writing dead pages, and replace the fixed 50 K hold with a clean-reserve rule.
- **Missing from both ideas: the SSD tier's own eviction.** The cleaner deletes the oldest-written pages first. Those are the shared prefix heads that live sessions keep using from memory. All 48 head-missing lookups after the first pass came from sessions with such a head; 73 % of all sessions have one. At that pass, finished sessions held 16.2 M tokens of written KV and live ones 4.7 M.
- **Metrics:** once the 128-user cap binds, the GPU pool stays 96-98 % full. Storage changes that do not cut recompute then mostly move waiting between requests that read and requests that don't (inferred). The paper should report the TTFT of requests that read, p90 and SSD volume, as well as the mean.
designs.fetch_rule:
**Statement.** Each read i is a job with a size (p_i missing pages) and a deadline d_i, set at a low quantile of its need time T_i = G_i + W_i; after arrival T_i is nearly a point.

- The I/O scheduler holds every known job: arrived reads, plus candidates before arrival as tentative jobs.
- It computes latest starts backward in deadline order, over the read rate left after writes (beta_r = beta - w):
  - s_i = min(d_i, s_next) - p_i * b / beta_r, where s_next is the start of the next job by deadline.
  - Every job due by d_i can then finish by d_i.
- A read is dispatched at its latest start, which keeps host memory free. It goes earlier only when the device would otherwise sit idle.
- Arrived reads always qualify. A read before arrival qualifies only if both hold:
  1. It fits in device slack: dispatching it now pushes no arrived read past its deadline.
  2. Its room comes from free pages or evict-first classes (ended sessions, clean duplicates), and its expected saved stall, P(T_i < D_r + r_i | idle time) * r_i, beats the eviction cost of the marginal victim.

**How G and W enter.**
- T = G + W.
- G comes from the hint distribution conditioned on idle time, and is 0 after arrival.
- W before arrival must be projected to the predicted arrival: queued GPU work plus expected arrivals. Today the engine uses the wait a request arriving now would see.
- Deadlines use a low quantile of T, so latest starts stay safe when the estimator lags. In campaign 34 jit_exact, the position x rate estimate was a median 19.8 s short for 30-60 s waits (ntp_admit lines; sim-calibration finding).

**How r and the storage queue enter.** r_i = D_r(d_i) + p_i * b / beta_r.
- D_r is the device time of jobs ahead of i in deadline order: parked reads, reads in flight, and 'now' reads expected before d_i.
- beta_r excludes the write rate. At saturation in campaign 34, writes took about 4.3 K tokens/s, about 0.42 GB/s of about 2.1 GB/s (campaign34/checks/fix_minutes.out, read_thread.out). While the write hold is on, beta_r = 0 for timed reads.
- Today the estimate before arrival counts only pages in flight (unified_radix_cache.py:2334-2337). The hold counts the parked pages ahead in the current pass (next_turn_prefetch.py:1448-1481). Neither counts writes or 'now' reads still to come.
- In campaign 34, reads due at once waited a median 30 s parked.

**What it reduces to, by regime.**
1. **W much larger than r, device has slack** (TraceLab on Triton): latest start = T - r - margin, which is today's hold. Reads before arrival never qualify.
2. **Device saturated** (campaign 28; campaign 34 from minute 70 for jit_p50 and minute 90 for the others): latest starts are already past, so reads run back to back in deadline order and holds never bind. Nothing before arrival qualifies. The lever is read demand (host room), not timing.
3. **W < r with device slack** (campaign 26 at 44 users): arrived reads start at once. Reads before arrival go on hint quantiles, gated by room. This is the only regime with a measured gain: 0.14-0.21 s with exact hints (campaign26/DECISIONS.md:835-876).
4. **Idle GPU, busy device:** recompute short histories. On an idle FA3 GPU, 20 K tokens recompute in about 0.62 s against a 0.8-1.1 s read (campaign32/checks/mechanisms_findings.txt:174).

**What is new against the engine today.**
- One r from the I/O scheduler, used by the planner, the hold and refetch.
- Latest starts computed backward over all jobs, replacing the per-read hold.
- The write rate inside r.
- Reads before arrival gated by device slack and evict-first room, instead of lambda (expected_cost) or early_s (just_in_time).
- W projected to the arrival time.

**Evidence.**
- Campaign 34, minutes 90-110: returning requests with an SSD read waited 45.6-68.7 s; the others waited 11.7-19.4 s. Their read stall is nearly their whole wait (45.0 of 45.6 s for ec_full), so the read line, not the GPU, set their admission (out/read_vs_noread_*.out).
- The read thread was 100 % busy from minute 70 (jit_p50) and minute 90 (ec_full, jit_exact), with reads parked 37-67 s (campaign34/checks/read_thread.out).
- jit_p50's 1,208 early reads raised SSD volume to 82.5 M tokens, against 64.1 M (ec_full) and 54.4 M (jit_exact), and held 95-241 K staged host tokens (out/census_windows_jit_p50.out).
- ec_full had W >= r in 3,929 of its 3,973 'arrival' decisions.
- Campaign 29's hold: -77.7 s, confounded with the arrival gate and the 120 s lead (campaign29/DECISIONS.md:210-232).

Scratch outputs are in /tmp/claude-1001/-home-wanhr-sglang/cf65791c-c7d4-4411-be47-21b43c92b26f/scratchpad/wf_design/designer-storage/out/.
designs.eviction_and_writes:
**Page states (OS page-cache view).**
- Pinned: landed reads until admission (budget 0.3 x pool), anchors of lookups and of parked or in-flight reads, and load-back sources.
- Dirty: an SSD write is pending; the page is host-locked from submit to ack (unified_radix_cache.py:2027-2061, 3504-3524).
- Clean: host-only and already on the SSD.
- Clean duplicate: a host copy of KV that is still on the GPU.

Campaign 34 census, minutes 30-110 (out/census_windows_*.out; campaign34/DECISIONS.md:98-102):
- clean duplicates 0.64-0.65 M tokens;
- clean host-only 0.87-0.98 M;
- dirty median 0-7 K (p90 65-94 K);
- pins 0-54 K;
- jit_p50's staged reads 95-241 K;
- parked-read anchors up to 107 K.

The clean duplicates equal the GPU tokens of running requests from minute 30 (0.64-0.65 M against 0.65 M; out/mirror_vs_running_*.out). Host eviction never takes them, because the host-leaf test requires node.evicted (unified_tree_core.py:2138-2158).

**One eviction order, by slack.** Evict the page group with the largest slack, T - (D_r + r): the least chance of being needed before it could be brought back. D_r is the read line's current delay. Never evict negative slack, pinned or dirty pages.

In class terms:
1. Ended sessions.
2. Clean duplicates of running requests. They are recreated by a D2H copy at finish, and only for sessions whose next T is short.
3. Idle prefixes, largest T first. This is where the forecast acts.
4. Staged reads, ordered by F(D_r + r). This is the draft's Preempt.
5. Queued requests farthest from admission, only while the read line can bring them back in time.
6. Never: the head of the queue.

Retain and Preempt become one rule.

The replay (out/host_room_replay_*.out) is open-loop, holds the recorded timeline fixed, and works at session level. Its write-through + LRU arm comes within about 20 % of the recorded SSD volumes.
- Without the mirror, SSD read demand falls from 63.3/62.7/56.6 M to 24.6/24.6/24.7 M tokens. That is the same as adding 0.65 M tokens of host memory.
- A perfect next-use order with session ends saves 22-25 % with the mirror, and a further 40-43 % without it. Forecasts matter more once host room is not wasted.
- Ordering the queued class farthest-first moves volume by under 1 %. The model cannot see timing.

Engine seams:
- Duplicate reclaim exists only under write_back (unified_tree_core.py:1739-1765).
- write_back blocks the scheduler on each D2H copy at GPU eviction (unified_radix_cache.py:983-990, 3745-3758).
- Under write_through, a GPU-evicted node with no host copy is deleted (unified_tree_core.py:1630-1640).
- An SSD lookup needs a host-backed anchor (scheduler.py:3160-3167).

Preempt has no evidence on FA3: 0 bumps in campaigns 32 and 34, and 462 in campaign 26 with no TTFT gain shown. It should not be a headline rule.

**Write path.** Keep eager write-through to the SSD:
- KV pages are immutable and append-only.
- 56-67 % of prompt positions are read back from the SSD at least once, each 4.2-4.5 times (out/client_writes_*.out).
- Eviction must stay instant. Campaign 32's loop came from dirty pages: 240-675 K tokens pending (campaign32/DECISIONS.md:163-191).

Changes:
- **(a) Skip dead pages.** In this replay the next prompt carries the recorded reply, not the generated tokens. Only 54 of about 16,400 next prompts reuse the previous output, so 4.78 M of the 31.6-31.9 M tokens submitted per run (15 %) are output KV that is never read (h2s_submit sums). The plan key includes this dead tail too (unified_radix_cache.py:1235-1241). Make output skipping a per-harness flag learned from the next turn's match. Also skip the last turn of ended sessions.
- **(b) Order queued writes by eviction rank instead of FIFO,** so the eviction frontier becomes clean first. This matters only when writes fall behind; the median write takes 0.1-0.6 s in campaign 34.
- **(c) Set the on-SSD state only when the ack covers the whole write.** Today a failed write releases the lock as if it had succeeded (unified_radix_cache.py:3511-3515).
- **(d) Keep fixes 1 and 2.**

**Writes against reads.**
- At saturation, reads ran at 17.4-18.0 K tokens/s and writes at about 4.3 K tokens/s on a device that tops out near 2.1 GB/s. Writes are mandatory at that rate, so priority can only smooth bursts; reducing volume is the real lever.
- I/O classes, highest first:
  1. 'now' reads;
  2. deadline reads, by latest start;
  3. frontier writes, when the clean reserve is short;
  4. reads before arrival, only in device slack;
  5. other writes.
- Replace fix 3's fixed 50 K hold with a dirty limit in the style of Linux dirty_ratio. Fix 3 switched on 28-30 times a run, for 57-81 s in total. The new rule holds timed reads only when free plus clean evictable room outside protected classes falls below the allocation expected over the write drain time (pending write tokens divided by the write rate).
- At this setting the new rule would change nothing. It matters for smaller hosts or faster GPUs.

**SSD tier.**
- How it fails today:
  - The cleaner deletes the page groups with the oldest mtime, from 90 % down to 80 % full (nixl_cleaner.py:168-212).
  - mtime changes only on writes and on fix 1's touch.
  - A lookup stops at the first missing page (hicache_nixl.py:658-664).
- Shared prefix heads are written once by the first session and then served to later sessions from GPU or host, so they are the oldest files.
- The evidence (out/head_missing_*.out, out/ssd_dead_live_*.out):
  - All 48 head-missing requests after the first pass (17/16/15 per arm) came from sessions whose first prompt shared a prefix with an older session; the shared part was a median 20-32 % of that prompt. Across all sessions the rate is 73 %, so 48 of 48 by chance has odds of about 3e-7.
  - 46 of the 48 sessions were younger than the window the passes deleted.
  - At the first pass, finished conversations held 16.2-16.3 M tokens of written KV and live ones 4.7 M. Each pass deletes about 2.5 M.
- Proposal:
  - Keep an in-memory index of stored pages: key, parent key, last use, and the live sessions holding the page. That is about 400 K pages, tens of MB.
  - Delete leaf-first: never a page with a stored descendant.
  - Delete ended or expired sessions first, then by last use or largest T.
  - Never delete pages with a parked or in-flight read. 31 'No such file' read failures came within 3 minutes of a pass.
- Touching files on read does not protect shared heads, because they are used from memory, not read from the SSD.
designs.paper_structure:
1. **Problem statement.** TTFT ≈ W + S + recompute, and W responds to recompute (keep section 2 of the design note). State the resources as they really are:
   - host room R depends on the mirror policy, and under write-through the mirror is the running set's KV;
   - one SSD of about 2.1 GB/s is shared by reads and writes;
   - the SSD tier has finite capacity and evicts on its own.
2. **Design: one memory-hierarchy manager with four components,** each with its rule and evidence.
   - (a) Time-to-use estimator: T = G + W, and r from the I/O queue.
   - (b) Host memory manager: page states and one slack order that covers retain, preempt and queued protection, with the mirror reclaimed.
   - (c) I/O scheduler: deadline reads with backward latest starts, reads before arrival only in device slack, and the write path (skip stored, merge, skip dead pages, clean-reserve hold).
   - (d) SSD tier: leaf-first, session-aware cleaning.
   - One figure: a session's prefix moving through the tiers on a timeline, with its page state.
   - One table: component, rule, engine seam, evidence.
   - lambda becomes one sentence: the marginal victim's eviction cost.
3. **Appendix.** Move there:
   - the per-session cost model and the newsvendor threshold;
   - the retention index and the dual bound, if kept;
   - the FA3 cost fits;
   - the replay and simulation models.
4. **Drop or rewrite these claims.**
   - "Storage holds every prefix cache" (design.tex:99). It is false once the volume fills (campaign 34: first pass at minute 88).
   - r_i = bL_i/beta. The read line dominates: reads were parked 17-67 s in campaign 34.
   - "Beyond b/(2 rho beta) reading is cheaper, and agentic contexts easily pass it." On FA3 the crossover is about 33-37 K tokens, above the 24.9 K mean history (inferred), and it depends on load.
   - "A read holds L_i tokens from its start." Parked reads hold only an anchor; pages are allocated at dispatch.
   - The price update as a main section: lambda never moved on FA3 (campaigns 32 and 34).
   - "Recency is a weak proxy": no TTFT gain from forecast-based eviction was shown in any campaign.
   - Preempt as a separate rule.
   - Any claim that reads before arrival carry the gain. They are shown only in campaign 26 at 44 users with exact hints, 0.14-0.21 s.
5. **Add these.**
   - The mirror and queue-room finding.
   - The write path as a design component. Campaign 34 against campaign 32 is -5.8 to -9.5 s, the largest measured effect on FA3.
   - The chain-aware SSD tier.
6. **Evaluation.** Report:
   - SSD read volume and read-line use;
   - TTFT of requests that read, and p90;
   - throughput;
   - the host census over time.
   Mark where the 128-user cap binds (minute 84-85). After it the box is a closed loop with a full GPU, and the mean is pinned by GPU throughput.

experiments.name: E1 Host room: the mirror against eviction order
experiments.question: How much of the SSD read demand at 128 users comes from the write-through mirror, and how much can eviction order win back?
experiments.method: CPU, offline. A first version is done: scratch scripts/host_room_replay2.py, outputs in out/host_room_replay_*.out. It replays the three campaign 34 timelines open-loop. Arrival and admission come from entry_time and queue_duration in server.log; finish and history (ideal_cached) come from client.jsonl. Host pool is 1.61 M tokens, with session-level units. Arms: mirror counted (write-through) or not (exclusive); LRU with queued last, queued farthest first, or oracle next use with session ends; plus write-through with 0.65 M more host memory as a control. Next steps: page-level prefixes with shared heads and leaf-only eviction; campaign 32's six runs and the running hicache rerun; and a read line of 17.5-21.5 K tokens/s that turns demand into lateness.
experiments.expected: First version, per run: write-through with LRU needs 56.6-63.3 M tokens of SSD reads, within about 20 % of the recorded 53.0-67.3 M. Exclusive needs 24.6-24.7 M (-56 to -61 %), the same as adding 0.65 M of host memory. Oracle next use with ends saves 22-25 %, and both together save 74-78 %. Under exclusive tiering, late-run demand is 7.5-7.9 K tokens/s, below the read line's 17.5 K.
experiments.decides: Whether reclaiming the mirror comes first among engine changes, and whether forecast-based eviction gets main-text space or becomes a tie-break.

experiments.name: E2 Closed-loop effect on TTFT
experiments.question: With the GPU full and the 128-user cap binding, does cutting SSD reads move mean TTFT, or only the TTFT of requests that read and the p90?
experiments.method: CPU discrete-event model. A closed-loop client replays the 729 users with recorded waits (gap cap 1,200 s, cap 128). The GPU is bound by its 668 K-token pool, with FA3 costs from the campaign 32/34 fits: prefill 0.0374 ms/token plus 27-35 ms per batch plus a prefix term; decode 3.5 + 0.47 x running + 0.016 x context-K ms. The host model is E1's. One read line shares 2.1 GB/s with writes, and admission is wait_complete. Arms: write-through against exclusive. Validate on campaign 34's per-minute request counts, queue lengths, and the waits of requests with and without a read.
experiments.expected: After minute 85, mean TTFT barely changes because the GPU is the bottleneck. The wait of requests with a read falls from 46-69 s toward the 12-19 s of requests without one, and p90 falls. Before the cap binds (minutes 60-85), mean TTFT falls by the share of stall that reads cause.
experiments.decides: Which metrics the paper reports for storage changes, and whether a GPU run of exclusive tiering justifies the engine work: an async D2H at GPU eviction or at finish, and SSD lookups from GPU-only anchors.

experiments.name: E3 Write volume and dirty memory by write policy
experiments.question: How much SSD write bandwidth do dead pages and eager writes cost, and is delayed write-through safe?
experiments.method: CPU replay of page chains per conversation, from client.jsonl plus the h2s_submit lines (node, tokens, time) of the three campaign 34 logs. Arms: eager write-through, validated against the 31.6-31.9 M tokens submitted per run; skip outputs that are never re-sent; skip the last turn of ended sessions; delayed write-through, writing a page when it nears E1's eviction frontier. Track the dirty tokens over time against a clean-reserve rule.
experiments.expected: Outputs are 15 % of writes in this replay. Ended sessions' last turns are a few percent. Delayed writes save more, but during bursts they need dirty memory well above the 50 K hold.
experiments.decides: Keep eager write-through. Build dead-page skipping as a per-harness learned flag. Drop write-back from the plan unless the dirty set stays bounded.

experiments.name: E4 SSD cleaning order
experiments.question: Which cleaning order stops live sessions from losing their SSD chains?
experiments.method: CPU replay of stored pages. Page keys come from token chains, shared heads included, written in h2s_submit order; lookups come from s2h_query. Simulate the volume as run (about 25 M tokens) and at 12 M and 6 M, to emulate a long-running service. Orders: oldest write first (today's; it must reproduce the 48 zero-head and 18 partial losses after the first pass); oldest write plus touch on read; leaf-first by last use; leaf-first with ended sessions first.
experiments.expected: Touch on read leaves shared heads exposed, because they are used from memory and never read. Leaf-first removes the zero-head losses. With ended sessions first, no live page is deleted at 25 M (16.2 M dead against 4.7 M live at the first pass), and most losses disappear at 6-12 M.
experiments.decides: Whether to build an in-memory index of stored pages for the cleaner, and whether the SSD tier gets its own design subsection.

experiments.name: E5 Device scheduling at saturation
experiments.question: With reads and writes on one 2.1 GB/s device, how much do I/O priority and backward scheduling change how late reads land?
experiments.method: CPU discrete-event model of the read line (deadline-ordered parked queue, 512-page window, FIFO read thread) and the write thread, sharing 2.1 GB/s. Feed it campaign 34's minutes 60-120: reads from srs_park (time, pages, deadline) and writes from h2s_submit. Arms: as run (FIFO writes, 50 K hold); writes yield to deadline reads under a clean-reserve limit; outputs not written; reads before arrival only in device slack.
experiments.expected: Priority helps only during bursts. Saturation persists, because writes are mandatory at about 4.3 K tokens/s. Skipping outputs adds a few percent of read rate. Reads land on time mainly when read demand falls (E1).
experiments.decides: Whether an I/O priority layer belongs in the design, or a clean-reserve hold is enough.

experiments.name: E6 Read-time estimator
experiments.question: How far is the engine's r from how long a read actually takes, and does a backward estimate in deadline order close the gap?
experiments.method: Offline over the campaign 34 logs. For each read, compare the load estimates at the plan and at the hold (ntp_hold, ec_start) with the time from park to landing (srs_park, srs_dispatch, s2h_io). Recompute r at park time from the parked pages ahead in deadline order, the pages in flight, the write-hold state and the measured read rate.
experiments.expected: Today's r misses the parked time, a median 17-30 s late in the run. The backward estimate lands within a few seconds, outside write-hold episodes.
experiments.decides: The r term of the unified fetch rule, and whether latest-start times replace the per-read hold.

risks: Exclusive tiering means changing the tree core. Under write_through, a GPU-evicted node with no host copy is deleted (unified_tree_core.py:1630-1640). The existing write_back path blocks the scheduler on each D2H copy (unified_radix_cache.py:983-990, 3745-3758). SSD lookups need a host-backed anchor (scheduler.py:3160-3167). Copying back at finish costs about 6 GB/s of D2H at about 2.3 requests/s (inferred). Scheduler stalls could cancel the room gained.

The host-room replay is open-loop and session-level. It holds W fixed and ignores shared prefixes, partial eviction, pins and read timing. The -56 to -61 % is a first-order estimate, not a prediction of TTFT.

Once the user cap binds, the box is a closed loop with a 96-98 % full GPU pool. Changes that do not cut recompute may leave mean TTFT flat and move only the tail (inferred). The paper has to choose its metrics with that in mind.

Dead output KV is an artifact of the replay: next prompts carry recorded replies, so only 54 of about 16,400 reuse the generated output. Real harnesses usually re-send outputs, so the 15 % write saving may not transfer. The artifact also inflates writes in every arm, and the plan key carries the dead tail. That tail may explain some ntp_reevict events; not traced.
Delayed write-through or write-back risks campaign 32's loop, where dirty pages blocked eviction and pending writes reached 240-675 K tokens. A hard dirty limit tied to the clean reserve is required.

SSD-tier effects appear only after the volume fills (minute 88 in a 2 h run). Testing the cleaner order needs lowered watermarks or longer runs, which change the regime. The page index must be rebuilt after a restart.
There is one run per arm and no measured spread in the saturated part. Campaign 34's arms differ by at most 0.7 s.

Backward scheduling relies on deadlines, and W predicted from position x rate lags a growing queue (a median 19.8 s short for 30-60 s waits). Latest starts can land late unless a conservative quantile is used.
Once dispatched, reads go to one FIFO read thread, and 'now' reads bypass the 512-page window. Any priority scheme can reorder only the parked queue.
The brief names Qwen3-32B-FP8. Campaigns 28-34 actually ran Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 with bf16 KV, 98,304 B per token. Any b/beta figure in the paper must use the latter.

verdicts.item: The gain comes from both pre-arrival reads and the queue-delay-based read schedule, so both timings belong in the fetch decision
verdicts.reason: Both effects were measured, but at very different sizes. At 44 users / 70 GB on Triton (campaign 26), the no-hint queue-aware engine reached 0.71-0.72 s against HiCache's 5.47-6.62 s, and exact hints added only 0.14-0.21 s (agent_cache/results/campaign26/DECISIONS.md:338-346, 632-633). On FA3 with the fixes, ec_full staged 1 read before arrival and tied jit_exact, which staged 99 (-0.06 s [-0.19, +0.06], campaign34/DECISIONS.md:147). Reads timed on p50 hints cost 0.6-0.9 s (campaign26/DECISIONS.md:895-937; campaign34/DECISIONS.md:143-155). One rule can carry both timings, with the pre-arrival case as its light-load corner.

verdicts.item: Model the queue wait as prefill work ahead, because position x rate lags a growing queue (sections 2 and 5)
verdicts.reason: Binned by its own prediction, the engine's position x rate (ntp_admit pred_wait_ql_ms) is unbiased for turns without their own read. The median error is -0.5 to +0.2 s up to 20 s predicted in all three campaign 34 arms, and -0.2 s overall in campaign 32 ec_full through the loop. The errors are elsewhere. Readers wait a median 8.4-27.3 s longer than predicted (the read line). Non-readers wait 7-20 s less at 20-60 s predicted, because the readers ahead of them are passed over. For readers, max(arrival + position x rate, own last landing) gives a median error of +0.4-0.5 s (|err| p90 3.0-4.0 s), against a p90 of 24-52 s for position x rate alone. A prefill sum models neither effect, and admission is bound by the KV pool at 19-23 running requests. verdicts.item: Class 4 (staged reads) is evicted before class 5 (queued), and 'a page cannot leave host memory until it is on the SSD'

verdicts.item: Toy results: release rules tie when memory is ample (27.2-27.4 s); pull K=2 beats the hold by 16 s when it is tight; light load ranks exact early reads 0.12 s, hold 0.26 s, p10 reads 1.65 s
verdicts.reason:
These are toy results only.
- The 16 s is pull2 against the hold (30.05 vs 46.34 s). The proposed unified rule (uni_ec) gave 35.32 s in the current code. An earlier code version (set2, no longer reproducible from the file) gave 91.42 s.
- The toy locks queued histories, and a refusal recomputes the whole history. The engine evicts queued-tier prefixes before refusing (python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/unified_radix_cache.py:3039-3047).
- There is no GPU mirror and no write path.
- ec_dist matches pre_exact to every printed digit in both saturated regimes. Its 1 s gap to the hold is likely the tick's second dispatch() call, not early reads (inferred from the code). The seed sd is 2.1 s.
- The toy's 2.33 req/s is compared with c34's whole-run 2.36 req/s. The late phase, whose 27 s TTFT the toy matches, ran at 2.16-2.22 req/s (campaign34/checks/by_minute_*.out, minutes 90-109).

Position x rate is already unbiased for non-readers, as in the design-note verdict above. I did not re-check the drift figure (0.9 s over 1 s).

verdicts.item: Replace the time hold with release by ready position (pull, small K)
verdicts.reason: Nothing in the engine logs supports it. Under saturation the hold barely binds: ec_full's first holds had a median of 3.8 s, and the last landing came a median 0.8 s before admission (agent_cache/results/campaign34/checks/read_waits_ec_full.out). Pull moves more waiting onto readers, who already wait 27-55 s longer in minutes 90-110. Its gain needs tight memory, and the engine's queued-tier eviction makes tight memory less harsh than in the toy. Keep it as a simulator arm.

critique.synthesis:
Repo paths are relative to /home/wanhr/sglang.

FETCH RULE
Treat each needed history as one read job. One function times it at both seams: _check_pending before arrival, and read_not_before / read_deadline after arrival.

Deadline and landing:
- The job's deadline D is when admission would take the turn if its history were resident. Its landing C comes from the read line.
- The structure is measured. For readers in campaign 34, max(arrival + position x rate, own last landing) predicts the wait to a median +0.4-0.5 s (|err| p90 3.0-4.0 s). Position x rate alone gives +8 to +27 s (p90 24-52 s). In campaign 32 ec_full: +0.4 s (p90 8.3 s) against +2.4 s (p90 14.7 s).

Estimators:
- Keep position x rate on the GPU side. Count a reader ahead only if its projected landing comes before the turn's slot; pass-over is why non-readers are over-predicted by 7-20 s at 20-60 s.
- Project C from the parked and in-flight pages in deadline order, at the read thread's measured ms/page, plus the write-hold state. Planned r was 8.3 s against 30-52 s actual in c34 jit_p50.
- Do not build the design note's prefill work-ahead W or the ready-only count; neither captures these two effects.

Choosing the release time:
- Use the argmin with recourse that read_start already computes, over c_L x E[lateness] + lambda x L x E[earliness].
- c_L is the chance the GPU has no other ready work when the turn reaches the front. It is about 1 at light load and about 0 once the KV pool is full with ready work queued, which holds in c34 from minute 30. EC's GPU-bound filter is the binary version.
- Before arrival, feed in the gap support conditioned on idle time. After arrival, G = 0.
- Under saturation this makes no early reads. At light load it reads early only with room that evicts nothing but ended sessions (or clean duplicates).
- Never use the threshold form: the trace's gap entries have falling hazards.

Pre-arrival reads are this rule's light-load corner. Exact hints added 0.14-0.21 s in campaign 26; realistic hints showed nothing; p50 timing cost 0.6-0.9 s. Lambda stays a fixed knob or comes from measured slack; harm learning never moved on FA3. Pull release and backward latest starts stay simulator arms.

EVICTION AND WRITES
The largest host lever on record is room, not order. Under write-through, host memory always mirrors the GPU pool: 0.65 M of 1.63 M tokens at 160 GB, and 668K of 712K at campaign 26's 70 GB, which left 44K of room. There, 30 GB more memory bought 0.52 s, more than any hint. Decide the mirror first, by CPU replay and then a GPU smoke. The options are dropping mirror copies whose SSD write has acked, or the existing write_back mode with the host-anchor rule relaxed.

Then rank every host holder in one list (idle histories, staged pins, queued histories beyond a protected head):
- Order by slack: a low quantile of T minus restore time.
- Restore is a read when an acked SSD copy exists. Otherwise it is a recompute priced at mu, which is much larger than 1 under saturation, so only copies stay.
- Ended sessions go first. Never evict pinned, in-flight, dirty or near-head pages.
- Expect at most 0.1 s from the ranking itself.
- Mark a page clean only when the ack covers the whole op.

Writes:
- Keep eager write-through to the SSD: 56-67 % of prompt positions are read back, 4.4-4.5 times each.
- Keep fixes 1 and 2.
- Read the end signal at insert and skip ended sessions' last turn.
- Skip never-reused output KV only behind a learned per-harness flag, since this is a replay artifact.
- Turn fix 3 into a write-against-read priority tied to the room the next due reads need.

With the fixes, pending writes hold a median 0-7K tokens. The write path is a stability component (campaign 32 -> 34: -5.8 to -9.5 s), not a consumer of room; its real host cost is the write-through mirror.

SSD tier:
- Never delete a page with stored descendants of a live session.
- Delete ended sessions' chains first.
- Refresh shared heads when memory matches them. All 48 zero-head losses had a shared head, against 65-66 % of page-0 lookups that hit, so touch-on-read alone does not fix them.

PAPER
Design in five parts:
1. T = G + W, with two coupled queues and the max(GPU turn, landing) structure.
2. Read release (deadline order, pins until admission, the hold) as the main mechanism, with the argmin as its rule and pre-arrival reads as its light-load case.
3. Host memory manager: mirror accounting, one ranking, ended sessions.
4. I/O path and stability: ration by delay, not refusal; the write fixes as instances, crediting the upstream precedent (Mooncake skips rewrites) as the note does.
5. SSD tier.

Answers to the design note's open questions:
- GPU time is priced at much more than 1 under saturation (about N once the user cap binds), with no learned second price. The Lagrangian goes to the appendix, as a decision rule, not a bound.
- Queued histories beyond the head may yield, last.

Evaluation:
- State the served model: Qwen3-30B-A3B, bf16 KV.
- Explain that after the 128-user cap binds, mean TTFT follows GPU throughput (Little's law; campaign 32 against 34, minutes 90-109).
- Report readers' TTFT, p90, requests per minute and slot wait, and mark the cap minute.
- Regimes: light load (campaign 26); GPU-saturated (campaigns 28/29, campaign 34 minutes 30-70); both saturated (campaign 34 minutes 90-110); host cliff (campaign 32).

Drop:
- the threshold rule;
- 'a read started at arrival completes before the head';
- 'storage holds every prefix';
- 'recency is a weak proxy';
- retention-index gains;
- the multiplicative price;
- Triton's b/(2 rho beta) constants;
- the unsourced numbers.
